DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) initiated this docket 
to improve equity, accessibility, and stakeholder engagement (EASE) in PURA 
proceedings. This proceeding identified key opportunities for PURA’s public engagement 
approach, and input from stakeholders helped provide a foundation for improving how 
underserved communities interact with the regulatory process. Through public meetings, 
surveys, and written comments, stakeholders highlighted persistent barriers that inhibit 
meaningful participation—such as confusing docket materials, limited public awareness, 
scheduling conflicts, and lack of available resources to support participation, such as 
childcare and translation services. Stakeholder input revealed that communities seek 
simpler communications, including informative videos and answers to frequently asked 
questions; consistent outreach through trusted messengers; and more accessible 
outreach, such as more hybrid and after-hours meetings, accessible venues, and real-
time translation. 
Although the Authority does not adopt every stakeholder recommendation, it is 
clear that building an inclusive, equitable engagement strategy requires investment in 
accessible communication, community partnerships, and internal capacity to support 
broader stakeholder participation across all PURA proceedings. The barriers to 
meaningful participation have many origins and were not formed overnight, and making 
improvements to EASE in PURA proceedings requires sustained effort and collaboration 
by PURA staff and stakeholders. Additionally, the Authority is a quasi-judicial agency 
statutorily charged with ensuring that Connecticut's investor-owned utilities, including the 
state’s electric, natural gas, water, and telecommunications companies, provide safe, 
clean, reliable, and affordable utility service and infrastructure. Some stakeholder 
recommendations with merit require legislative approval or legislative appropriation 
before PURA can act. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
The Authority initiated this proceeding to identify improvements that can be made 
to equity and accessibility in proceedings before the Authority, as well as PURA’s 
communication with stakeholders. The Authority sought to improve opportunities for 
participation in the decision-making processes, especially by low-income residential 
customers, residential customers that experience high energy burdens, and individuals 
and communities impacted by Authority decisions. 
Through this proceeding, the Authority sought stakeholder input regarding the 
barriers that hinder effective participation and engagement, opportunities to improve 
stakeholder participation and engagement in dockets, methods to help the public better 
understand the industries PURA regulates, and what accessibility tools PURA and the 
public service companies should prioritize. 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 2

C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On September 17, 2024, the Authority initiated this proceeding to identify potential 
improvements to EASE in proceedings before the Authority. On October 3, 2024, the 
Authority provided notice of its intention to hire a consultant to support the EASE docket. 
The Authority subsequently engaged a team consisting of Common Spark Consulting, 
Elevated Engagement, and Dunsky Energy + Climate Advisors (Consultant Team). 
The Authority requested recommendations from participants and stakeholders for 
possible meeting locations, such as libraries, town halls, or other community spaces, for 
public meetings on March 20, 2025, and May 13, 2025. Notice of Request for 
Participation Recommendations, Oct. 8, 2025; Revised Notice of Request for Participant 
Recommendations, November 25, 2025. The Authority also requested recommendations 
to make these meetings more accessible to community members, by reducing the burden 
on community members’ attendance, including timing, provision of childcare, and transit 
access. 
Stakeholders suggested typically accessible locations, such as libraries, schools, 
community centers, and town halls, as well as specific locations. See Operation Fuel 
d/b/a Generation Power CT (GPCT) Corresp., Jan. 31, 2025; Nonprofit Accountability 
Group (NAG) Corresp., Jan.17, 2025; Aropa Consulting, LLC (Aropa) Corres., Feb. 19, 
2025. In addition, stakeholders recommended offering both hybrid and fully virtual 
meeting formats to support broader participation. See Office of Consumer Counsel 
(OCC) Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025. Stakeholders also proposed accessibility measures to 
make it easier for community members to engage in PURA proceedings, including 
adjustments to meeting times and measures to reduce participation burdens. 
The Authority held four noticed meetings to obtain participant and public input, 
each facilitated by the Consultant Team. Two of the meetings were held in person and 
two were held via remote teleconference. 
The first in person meeting took place in Hartford, on March 20, 2025, at the Center 
for Contemporary Culture at the Hartford Public Library. On May 13, 2025, the Authority 
hosted a second public meeting at the Ives Main Library in New Haven. The public 
meetings included discussions about PURA’s role, responsibilities, and current 
processes, as well as why PURA wants to expand access and stakeholder engagement. 
Attendees provided input about their interest in and ability to engage with the Authority, 
what issues at PURA matter to them, suggestions for improving accessibility in PURA 
proceedings, and recommendations to improve PURA’s outreach and engagement, 
including changes to the PURA website. 
The Authority held its first technical meeting, via remote teleconference, on April 
10, 2025, to discuss the highlights and input from the first public meeting and hear reports 
from stakeholder groups about the results of their stakeholder engagement and research 
during the course of this proceeding. On June 24, 2025, the Authority held a second 
technical meeting, via remote teleconference, to discuss the highlights and input from the 
second public meeting, as well as to provide an overview of the Stakeholder Group 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 3

Compensation Program. The Authority also received public and participant input during 
both technical meetings. 
Additionally, the Authority requested that participants and other stakeholders 
provide written comments in response to the following specific questions (EASE 
Questions): 
(1) How can PURA make stakeholder participation and engagement in dockets 
easier, more meaningful, and more efficient? 
(2) What constraints or obstacles currently limit effective participation and 
engagement? 
(3) What information can PURA provide to help consumers understand regulated 
services? 
(4) What accessibility tools, such as translation, should be prioritized by PURA and 
the public service companies? 
Notice of Request for Comments, Aug. 12, 2025, p. 1. The Authority received written 
comments from several stakeholders and participants. 
On November 4, 2025, the Consultant Team submitted a report, titled 
Strengthening Equity and Public Involvement at PURA (Consultant Report), which is 
contained in Appendix A: Consultant Report. 
On November 25, 2025, the Authority issued a proposed final decision and 
provided participants with an opportunity to file written exceptions. The Authority received 
written exceptions from (1) The Connecticut Natural Gas Corporation, The Southern 
Connecticut Gas Company, and The United Illuminating Company (collectively, Avangrid), 
(2) Aropa, (3) The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, 
Yankee Gas Services Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, and Aquarion Water Company 
of Connecticut (collectively, “Eversource Companies”), (4) OCC, (5) GPCT, and (6) the 
Center for Children Advocacy (CCA). 
D. 
PARTICIPANTS 
A list of participants is attached as Appendix B: Service List. 
II. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT 
Stakeholder engagement was fundamental to the progress of this docket, and the 
Authority received substantial input from docket participants and members of the public. 
Many docket participants contributed to the docket directly through correspondence and 
written comments. The Consultant Team also gathered input from stakeholders through 
interviews, small-group discussions, and its review of the comments and correspondence 
filed in this docket. Consultant Report, p. 6. 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 4

OCC submitted suggestions regarding improving public participation, noting that 
“although PURA’s topics might affect everyone’s daily lives, the topics might not rise to 
the forefront of what Connecticut customers pay attention to in their daily lives. . . . As a 
result, customer education might be necessary before meaningful customer engagement 
can be achieved.” OCC Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025, p. 1. OCC also suggested improving 
the accessibility of customer education, including using shorter programs, online 
resources, and more interactive discussions. Id., pp. 1–2. OCC subsequently noted 
several themes that arose during the course of the proceeding, including (1) PURA’s need 
for an updated and improved website, (2) the lack of fundamental understanding of PURA 
that many customers have, and (3) “that members of the public often do not have the time 
to meaningfully engage in PURA’s dockets even though they recognize that the work done 
in these dockets may affect their everyday lives.”1 OCC Comments, Aug. 22, 2025, pp. 
1–2. 
NAG extensively participated throughout this proceeding, both via written 
submissions and participation in meetings. In response to the EASE Questions, NAG 
conducted a community-based survey to identify barriers that limit effective public 
participation in PURA meetings. NAG Survey Report, p. 2. The results highlight a range 
of structural and logistical challenges that disproportionately affect underserved 
populations and offer actionable recommendations to reduce those burdens and increase 
accessibility, equity, and engagement. Id. NAG’s written submissions included the results 
of its survey and a variety of recommendations related to reducing attendance burdens; 
improving accessibility, equity, and engagement for underserved populations; and 
increasing public awareness of PURA and the industries it regulates. See generally NAG 
Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025 (containing two attachments with recommendations); NAG 
Comments, Aug. 1, 2025 (containing five attachments with recommendations).2 NAG’s 
recommendations are discussed in more detail in Section II.C, Barriers & Objectives, 
below. 
Although NAG’s initial comments were largely focused on providing 
recommendations for the public meetings in this docket, the survey results are also 
generally applicable to other PURA proceedings. NAG “conducted a survey among its 

1 As OCC notes, "OCC and other long-term stakeholders have voiced many of these suggestions for 
years." OCC Exceptions, p. 1. Although some of the ideas and recommendations in this docket may 
have been made by stakeholders, such as OCC, in the course of other dockets, this docket was an 
opportunity to gather more information and feedback from a broader community. As OCC acknowledges, 
"it is valuable to obtain outside perspectives to help improve access and equity in regulatory proceedings." 
Id., pp. 1–2. Through the extensive stakeholder contributions to this docket, the Authority was able to 
gather recommendations and understand various stakeholders' priorities, including the perspectives of 
stakeholders who have been historically unrepresented or underrepresented in prior proceedings. The 
Authority also commends OCC for using the feedback from this proceeding to create additional resources 
to help the public understand how to engage with PURA. See id., p. 2.

members to gather data on improving stakeholder participation. The survey covered four 
key areas: familiarity with PURA, accessibility and logistics, transit, transportation, and 
childcare, and equity and inclusion.” NAG Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025, Report on Enhancing 
Stakeholder Participation in PURA Decision-Making Processes (NAG Survey Report), p. 
2; see also NAG Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025, Improving Accessibility and Equity in PURA 
Public Meetings Testimony Docket # 24-09-07 (NAG Summary Report), p. 1. 
NAG subsequently provided written comments that consisted of five documents: 
(1) Recommendation for a PURA Proceeding to Improve Public Education on Existing 
Energy Assistance Programs, (2) The Critical Role of PURA’s Stakeholder Group 
Compensation Program and the Need for Clarity on “Substantial Contribution” (NAG 
Substantial Contribution Recommendations), (3) Recommendation to PURA: Implement 
Additional Targeted Initiatives to Improve Access and Close Service Gaps (NAG Targeted 
Initiatives Recommendations), (4) PURA Website Recommendations (NAG Website 
Recommendations), and (5) Statement of the Nonprofit Accountability Group in Support 
of its Participation in the EASE Docket (NAG EASE Report). NAG Corresp., Aug. 1, 2025. 
In this docket, NAG’s engagement has been informed by structured community focus 
groups and workshop sessions, designed to build familiarity with PURA’s role and ensure 
feedback is gathered in a manner consistent with the principles of procedural justice. 
NAG EASE Report, p. 1. The Authority agrees that “NAG’s participation in this docket 
enabled PURA to engage meaningfully with impacted constituencies to better craft policy 
solutions grounded in the realities of low-income ratepayers.” Id. 
Additionally, Aropa conducted a multi-phase stakeholder engagement effort as part 
of its participation in this proceeding, aimed at identifying the barriers, motivations, and 
opportunities for meaningful participation in PURA’s regulatory processes by small 
businesses, nonprofit organizations, and residential customers. Aropa Comments, Aug. 
21, 2025, p. 1. Aropa’s engagement primarily targeted communities within Greater New 
Haven and included four focus groups, one in-person and three virtual; three one-on-one 
virtual interviews with nonprofit and small business leaders in June 2025; and an online 
survey in May and June 2025, which yielded 65 complete responses from participants in 
various Connecticut towns. Id. Aropa notes that the information summarized in its report 
was anonymized from its stakeholder engagement effort. Id., p. 1. 
Aropa’s stakeholder engagement identified several key opportunities to improve 
the accessibility, transparency, and inclusiveness of PURA’s regulatory processes. Aropa 
Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 2. Stakeholders, particularly small businesses, nonprofit 
organizations, and historically underrepresented communities, expressed a desire for 
more meaningful engagement, while also noting consistent barriers such as low visibility, 
complex communications, rigid scheduling, and limited feedback mechanisms. Id. To 
address these concerns, Aropa makes recommendations regarding six issues: (1) 
increasing stakeholder awareness, (2) simplifying communications, (3) improving digital 
infrastructure, (4) diversifying meeting formats and schedules, (5) enhancing participant 
feedback loops, and (6) establishing ongoing support structures. Id., pp. 3–5. According 
to Aropa, these recommendations reflect a strategic roadmap for PURA to deepen public 
trust, enhance transparency, and foster a more equitable and community-centered 
approach to regulatory engagement. Id., p. 5. 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 6

The Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) makes several recommendations related 
to the EASE questions, which are detailed in Section II.C, Barriers & Objectives, below.3 
See CLF Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, pp. 1–4. CLF also submitted correspondence that 
included a report titled “Overly Impacted & Rarely Heard,” issued in May 2023 by the 
Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General Stakeholder Working Group. CLF 
Corresp., May 15, 2025. CLF summarized the seven sections of the report, including (1) 
advancing equity, (2) improving transparency and accountability, (3) improving 
information and knowledge accessibility, (4) reforming public engagement, (5) reforming 
intervention standards, (6) improving public hearings, evidentiary hearings and public 
meetings, and (7) recommendations related to adjudications. Id., pp. 2–6. 
GPCT emphasizes the importance of the ongoing efforts of PURA to educate the 
public and increase diversity among stakeholders participating in dockets. See GPCT 
Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 1. GPCT identifies several challenges to effective public 
participation and engagement in docketed proceedings and offers recommendations, 
which are discussed in Section II.C, Barriers & Objectives, below. Additionally, GPCT 
recommends that PURA revisit this stakeholder engagement docket every five years, 
potentially aligning with the schedule of bill design reviews,4 to maintain momentum and 
embed accessibility goals in long-term planning. Id., p. 5. 
CCA also emphasizes the importance of PURA’s commitment to improving public 
participation and notes that engagement of a broad, diverse range of stakeholders, 
particularly those unfamiliar with regulatory processes, requires “true communications 
expertise.” CCA Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025, p. 1. CCA also notes that the energy policy 
landscape is complex and many ratepayers find PURA’s language, procedures, and filing 
systems intimidating or inaccessible; as a result, uninitiated or vulnerable populations 
may either remain disengaged or be influenced by external sources that may not provide 
accurate information. Id. 
The Yankee Institute (YI) also recommends plain-language docket summaries, 
comprehensive notifications to customers about upcoming meetings and decisions, and 
enhanced communication strategies to customers to ensure awareness and encourage 
participation in proceedings. YI Corresp., Jan. 16, 2025, pp. 1–2. 
The Eversource Companies identify barriers to effective participation, including 
time constraints, lack of technical knowledge, and limited awareness, which could be 
mitigated through improved communication tools, simplified notices, and more intuitive 
access to public comment options. Eversource Companies Comments, Aug. 22, 2025, 
p. 3. The companies also express support for cost-effective accessibility enhancements, 
such as basic website translation features, closed captioning, and multilingual notices in 
select dockets. Id. The Eversource Companies recommend simplifying the process by 
using familiar public venues for in-person meetings and communicating logistics clearly. 

3 CLF also recognized NAG’s “valuable community-level input, including perspectives from low-income 
and environmental justice community residents” CLF Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 2. 
4 CCA also suggested revising utility bills to include information about PURA and how to engage with 
PURA. CCA Exceptions, p. 1. Such a bill revision could be best considered in the bill design review 
process.

Id. The Eversource Companies also recommend that any new working groups 
“complement, and not overlap with, existing” docket-specific “robust, structured 
engagement pathways,” such as is in Docket No. 21-05-15RE03, PURA Investigation into 
the Establishment of Integrated Distribution System Planning Within a Performance-
Based Regulation Framework. Eversource Companies Exceptions, p. 1–2. 
Avangrid supports the goals of this proceeding and commits to working towards a 
more accessible regulatory process, but Avangrid suggests that the solutions put forth to 
address the objectives of this proceeding will likely have associated costs. Avangrid 
Corresp., Jan. 16, 2025, p. 2; Avangrid Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 2. Avangrid 
recommends that proposed solutions be viewed through a cost-benefit lens to optimize 
outcomes for customers. Avangrid Corresp., Jan. 16, 2025, p. 2; Avangrid Comments, 
Aug. 21, 2025, p. 2. Avangrid suggests solutions for three discrete concerns, all focused 
on information accessibility and understandability. Avangrid Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, 
pp. 2–3. 
The Connecticut Water Company (CWC) notes the difficulty for all stakeholders 
and customers to participate in the current regulatory arena and recommends the 
following improvements to stakeholder education and engagement: (1) simplifying 
technical materials, (2) providing educational materials in large, easy-to-read print; (3) 
simplifying roles of docket participants; (4) increasing outreach to stakeholders; (5) 
distinguishing between major and minor dockets/proceedings; (6) utilizing utility websites 
as educational tools; and (7) using diverse communication channels, frequently, to 
describe the role of the Authority and its responsibilities. CWC Corresp., Feb. 3, 2025, p. 
2. CWC also recommends (1) distributing materials which are easy to understand, (2) 
hosting well-noticed events in a variety of times and locations which are accessible by 
public transportation, and (3) leveraging AI chat bots, live chat functions, and other online 
materials to reduce the barriers to the community. Id., pp. 3–4. 
B. 
IDENTIFICATION OF BARRIERS & PROPOSED IMPROVEMENTS (OBJECTIVES) 
The Consultant Team identified barriers and proposed improvements (objectives) 
by collaborating with PURA staff to conduct a preliminary assessment and facilitating 
information gathering in this docket (engaged research). As part of those processes, the 
Consultant Team met with PURA staff, including staff of the Authority’s Office of 
Education, Outreach, and Enforcement (EOE); facilitated four meetings open to 
participants and the public; and collecting input from stakeholders through interviews, 
small-group discussions, and the comments and correspondence filed in this docket. 
Consultant Report, p. 6. 
Stakeholders identified a range of challenges to engaging with the Authority, which 
the Consultant Team categorized into three barriers, relating to: (1) public awareness and 
understanding, (2) public input and impact, and (3) resources for public participation. 
Consultant Report, p. 7. The Consultant Team also identified objectives aimed at 
reducing each barrier. Consultant Report, pp. 10–11. For each objective, the Consultant 
Team proposed three broad recommendations and identified a variety of key actions. Id., 
pp. 11–25. Section II.C, Barriers & Objectives, below, explores the three major barriers 
identified by stakeholders and the Consultant Team’s proposed strategy. The Consultant

cost, and impact, as summarized in Figure 1 and Figure 2, below.

C. 
BARRIERS & OBJECTIVES 
1. Awareness of and Familiarity with PURA 
a. Barrier: Limited Public Awareness and Understanding of PURA 
The first barrier identified by the Consultant Team is that many people lack 
familiarity with PURA. Consultant Report, p. 7. Many Connecticut residents “are not 
aware of what PURA is, how PURA intersects with their lives, or the authority PURA has.” 
Id. Ratepayers’ awareness of PURA’s impact is often limited to their participation in utility 
affordability and assistance programs. Id. Even when organizations and individuals are 
interested in engaging with the Authority, they often do not know where to begin, or do 
not understand the legal requirements or constraints regarding participation. Id. Those 
stakeholders may not be able to easily navigate available information, as the language is 
often technical, bureaucratic, or out of date. The scarcity of plain language resources can 
be a significant barrier to new advocates’ understanding of how organizations and 
communities may be impacted by PURA. Id., pp. 7–8. 
In Aropa’s focus group sessions, one of the most consistent and foundational 
barriers identified by Aropa was the limited awareness and understanding of PURA’s role 
among small businesses, nonprofit leaders, and residential stakeholders. Aropa 
Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 9. Many focus group participants described their familiarity 
as “low” or “fair,” with some stating they had never heard of PURA prior to the engagement 
sessions or had only encountered it in the context of utility bills or rate increases. Id. 
Even among participants who had heard of PURA, there was widespread uncertainty 
regarding its regulatory functions, decision-making processes, and relevance to their 
communities. Id. Importantly, it appears that the lack of clarity was not simply due to 
unfamiliarity but rather reflected a broader perception of PURA as a distant and 
inaccessible institution. Aropa Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 9. This perception was 
echoed during one-on-one interviews, where individuals described PURA’s presence as 
largely reactive – only visible during contentious rate case proceedings – with little 
proactive engagement or tailored outreach to small stakeholders. Id., p. 11. 
Numerous stakeholders identify PURA’s website as a significant barrier to better 
familiarity with PURA and the regulatory process. GPCT notes that PURA’s website is a 
major obstacle to meaningful engagement, because of its confusing layout and lack of 
intuitive navigation features. GPCT Comments, pp. 5–6. Aropa also highlights 
stakeholders’ descriptions of the website as difficult to navigate and inaccessible. Aropa 
Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 4. 
GPCT also identifies several key constraints that limit effective stakeholder 
participation in PURA proceedings, particularly for ratepayers, non-profit organizations, 
and members of the public who wish to contribute meaningfully to the regulatory process. 
Id., p. 4. Specifically, GPCT emphasizes that the highly technical nature of regulatory 
topics continues to serve as a barrier to participation. Id. Additionally, GPCT notes that 
many stakeholders struggle to discern which energy issues fall under PURA’s jurisdiction 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 10

and how best to participate in those matters. Id. Similarly, OCC suggests that many 
customers do not understand what PURA does and that this misunderstanding “must be 
overcome for the public to know what can and cannot be accomplished in a PURA docket 
and the topics over which PURA does and does not have jurisdiction.” OCC Comments, 
Aug. 22, 2025, p. 1. 
Stakeholders also raise concerns about the availability and accessibility of 
community outreach efforts. For example, GPCT raises concerns about the outsized 
presence of utility staff at public and technical meetings, which may discourage public 
participation and create an unbalanced and intimidating environment for stakeholders. 
GPCT Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, pp. 2–3. Also, GPCT urges PURA to recognize the 
inherent structural advantages public service companies have, such as legal resources 
and regulatory expertise, and intentionally hold space for broader public engagement. 
Id., pp. 4–5. 
b. Objective: Increase Public Awareness and Understanding of PURA 
The Consultant Team proposed three recommendations that would further the 
objective of increasing public awareness and understanding of PURA, with specific focus 
on providing information about PURA that is clearer, more accessible, and inclusive. 
Consultant Report, pp. 11–18. Figure 3, below, summarizes the Consultant Team’s 
recommendations, including their assessment of (1) the level of control PURA has to 
make changes, without legislative or other authorization, (2) the expected cost, 
considering existing staff time and capacity, new staff, and other costs, and (3) the 
potential impact on equity and accessibility. See Consultant Report, pp. 10–11. 
Figure 3: Objective 1 Recommendations 

Consultant Report, p. 11. 
The Consultant Team’s recommendations are based on stakeholder input, such as 
Aropa’s finding, from its stakeholder engagement, of a widespread lack of awareness 
regarding PURA’s role and processes. See Aropa Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, pp. 14–15. 
Aropa’s survey results showed that 82% of respondents had never participated in a PURA 
proceeding, and 74% cited the technical complexity of materials as a key barrier to 
understanding. Id., p. 15. Aropa notes that focus group participants expressed strong 
interest in clearer, more accessible explanations of the Authority’s work, including through 
plain-language tools, real-world examples, and proactive outreach. Id., pp. 12–14. 

Docket No. 24-09-07 
Page 11

The recommendations are also responsive to stakeholder feedback that additional 
outreach efforts are necessary, both online and in person. Although expressing 
appreciation of PURA’s recent efforts to expand public understanding of regulated 
services, GPCT emphasizes that most members of the public remain unfamiliar with utility 
regulation and, therefore, additional tools are necessary to allow them to meaningfully 
understand and engage in PURA proceedings. GPCT Comments, Aug. 21, 2025, p. 5. 
GPCT highlights several initiatives, including the launch of a YouTube channel, live-
streamed decision meetings, PURA 101 roadshows across the state, and the publication 
of a quarterly newsletter, as important efforts to continue to demystify the regulatory 
process. Id. Similarly, OCC suggests that the Authority should maximize customer 
exposure to the helpful YouTube videos that the Authority has already made available. 
OCC Corresp., Jan. 17, 2025, p. 2. 
c. Recommendation: Enhance PURA Informational Resources 
First, the Consultant Team recommends that PURA enhance informational 
resources, including by developing more entry-level resources and consistently 
implementing accessibility best practices. Consultant Report, pp. 11–13. The Authority 
presents information online that is often technical and complex. Id., p. 11. The Consultant 
Team’s first “recommendation focuses on both 1) enhancing the presentation of 
information about PURA, and 2) ensuring that information is accessible to a wide range 
of audiences.” Id. 
Developing more resources that contain entry-level information, including 
information about PURA’s role in the regulation of utility services and specifically about 
the role of EOE staff, could provide ratepayers and stakeholders with a stronger 
foundational understanding of PURA and how PURA’s decisions may affect them.5 
Consultant Report, p. 11. For example, the Consultant Team suggests that an entry-level 
version of basics about PURA could be made available on the front page of the PURA 
website, including plain language explanations of important information, accompanied by 
“illustrative graphics and charts.”6 Id., pp. 11–12. The Authority could offer similar content 
“in different mediums, such as a slide deck with notes and resource links . . . or as [short] 
videos” hosted on a website like YouTube. Id., p. 12. 
The Consultant Team’s suggestions result from extensive stakeholder requests for 
more accessible information. For example, Aropa recommends simplifying 
communication by creating plain-language resources such as “PURA 101” one-pagers, 
FAQs, short videos, and infographics to clarify regulatory processes and encourage 

5 CCA emphasizes the need for PURA to provide clearer, more accessible information to help consumers 
understand their electric rates. CCA Corresp., Jan. 17., 2025, p. 2. CCA strongly recommends hiring a 
qualified communications expert who specializes in public engagement, particularly with populations that 
are financially vulnerable or disconnected from traditional information channels. CCA Corresp., Jan. 17, 
2025, p. 1. CCA suggests that the expert develop alternative, accessible communication strategies 
beyond the conventional tools such as bill stuffers, utility-controlled websites, and dense notices. Id. The 
goal is to make PURA’s processes understandable and inviting for broader public involvement, ensuring 
that all voices are heard and respected in regulatory decisions. Id.

2. Access to PURA 
a. Barrier: Limited Public Input and Impact 
The second barrier identified by the Consultant Team is the limited opportunity for 
public input, which results in stakeholders’ actual or perceived lack of impact on decision-
making. Consultant Report, p. 8. Although the public may participate in proceedings by 
(1) submitting public comments or (2) requesting official status in a docket (i.e., participant 
or intervenor status), many are unaware of how to contribute, uncertain as to when they 
may submit contributions, or are intimidated by the formality of the process. Additionally, 
many customer issues do not perfectly align with issues being addressed in an open 
docket, further complicating stakeholder efforts to identify the appropriate docket in which 
to participate. Id. Many members of the public who engage with PURA do so through 
EOE, which is responsible for customer support, education, and community engagement; 
however, EOE input regarding ratepayer concerns and challenges is often absent from 
docketed proceedings.17 Id., p. 19.

Glossary 
The following definitions are common in PURA interactions. Terms are provided in plain language to 
increase comprehension. When relevant, legal definitions are provided in footnotes. 
Case - (used interchangeably with “Docket” and “Proceeding”) 
Contested Proceeding1 - a formal process used to make decisions on utility requests and/or 
disputes. 
Docket - a virtual file drawer for all information contributed by people and organizations on a 
particular proceeding or case. Each is uniquely identified using a YY-MM-## format. Information 
submitted in a docket makes up "the record." 
Energy Burden - The percentage of a household’s income spent on energy costs. An energy 
burden of 6% or more is considered high and 10% or more is considered severe. 
Ex Parte Communication - Ex parte means by or from one party. An ex parte communication is 
when one person or group in a docket communicates with PURA without the presence, 
knowledge, or consent of all parties and intervenors. 
Intervenor2 - An individual or group approved by PURA to be involved in a contested proceeding. 
Participant3 - An individual or group approved by PURA to take part in some or all of the parts of 
an uncontested proceeding. 
Party4 - An individual or group in a Contested Proceeding who either (1) has filed a case with 
PURA to ask for something, (2) is required to participate by law, and/or (3) is essential to making 
a decision on the issues in the case. 
Proceeding - (used interchangeably with “Case” and “Docket”) 
1 Legal definition of Contested Case - “a proceeding, including but not restricted to rate-making, price fixing 
and licensing, in which the legal rights, duties or privileges of a party are required by state statute or 
regulation to be determined by an agency after an opportunity for hearing or in which a hearing is in fact 
held, but does not include proceedings on a petition for a declaratory ruling under section 4-176, hearings 
referred to in section 4-168 or hearings conducted by the Department of Correction or the Board of Pardons 
and Paroles.” (Section 4-166 of the Connecticut General Statutes). 
2 Legal definition of Intervenor - “a person, other than a party, granted status as an intervenor by an agency 
in accordance with the provisions of subsection (d) of section 4-176 or subsection (b) of section 4-177a” 
(Section 4-166 of the Connecticut General Statutes). 
3 Legal definition of “Participant” - any person granted permission by the Authority to take part in 
an uncontested proceeding (PURA Rules and Practice). 
4 Legal definition of Party - ”each person (A) whose legal rights, duties or privileges are required by statute 
to be determined by an agency proceeding and who is named or admitted as a party, (B) who is required by 
law to be a party in an agency proceeding, or (C) who is granted status as a party under subsection (a) of 
section 4-177a” (Section 4-166 of the Connecticut General Statutes).

Executive Summary 
The Connecticut Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA) is statutorily charged with ensuring 
that Connecticut utilities provide safe, clean, reliable, and affordable utility services at fair prices.7 
In September 2024, PURA opened the Equity, Accessibility, and Stakeholder Engagement 
(EASE) docket (Docket Number 24-09-07) to identify improvements that can be made to equity 
and accessibility in PURA proceedings and to PURA’s communication with stakeholders.8 In the 
EASE Docket, PURA focused on improving the opportunities for participation in the decision-
making process for low-income customers,9 residential customers with high energy burdens,10 
and individuals and communities impacted by Authority decisions. PURA also sought to identify 
stakeholders that have not previously engaged with PURA, to increase the spectrum of 
perspectives that are considered in decisions. 
In the EASE docket, PURA posed four questions to guide the work: 
1. How can PURA make stakeholder participation and engagement in dockets easier, more 
meaningful, and more efficient? 
2. What constraints or obstacles currently limit effective participation and engagement? 
3. What information can PURA provide to help consumers understand regulated services? 
4. What accessibility tools should be prioritized by PURA and the public service companies? 
PURA engaged Common Spark Consulting, Elevated Engagement, and Dunsky Energy + Climate 
Advisors (EASE consultant team) to support them with this work. Over the course of the project, 
the EASE consultant team engaged in research and met with PURA staff,11 community advocacy 
organizations, community members, and energy program providers to explore the answers to 
these four questions and produce recommendations that will help advance PURA’s goal— 
increase participation of underrepresented individuals and communities in PURA proceedings. 
The EASE consultant team’s research uncovered three broad barriers to more inclusive and 
effective participation and engagement: 
1. Low public awareness and understanding of PURA 
2. Limited ways for public input to contribute to and inform matters before PURA 
3. Significant resources are often required for participation in PURA proceedings

Chapter I. EASE Overview 
About the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority 
The mission of the Connecticut Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA) is to ensure that 
Connecticut utilities provide safe, clean, reliable, and affordable utility services at fair prices.12 
PURA provides regulatory oversight over utility services, including electricity, natural gas, water, 
telecommunications, and cable, television and video. 
PURA advances the state’s energy, economic, and environmental goals, which is critical to 
maintaining public health, safety, and a robust economy.13 
PURA is a quasi-judicial agency that interprets and applies statutes and regulations governing 
Connecticut’s utility sector. To make its decisions, PURA opens proceedings called “dockets” to 
discuss specific issues and cases. Like a court, PURA can only make decisions based on the 
evidence in the docket (often referred to as, “the record”). 
About the Equity, Accessibility, and Stakeholder Engagement 
Docket 
In September 2024, PURA opened the Equity, Accessibility, and Stakeholder Engagement (EASE) 
docket (Docket Number 24-09-07) to identify improvements that can be made to equity and 
accessibility in PURA proceedings and to PURA’s communication with stakeholders.14 In the 
EASE Docket, PURA focused on improving the opportunities for participation in the decision-
making processes for low-income customers,15 residential customers with high energy burdens,16 
and individuals and communities impacted by PURA’s decisions. PURA also sought to identify 
stakeholders that have not previously engaged with PURA, to increase the spectrum of 
perspectives that are considered in decisions (Callout Box 1). 
The goal of the EASE Strategy is to increase participation of underrepresented individuals and 
communities in PURA proceedings, ensuring that all stakeholders have a meaningful opportunity 
to contribute to and inform decisions and advance more equitable outcomes. In the EASE docket, 
PURA posed four questions to guide the work:17

Chapter III. Barriers 
Through each step of the strategy development process, the consultant team looked for 
impediments to access and meaningful engagement with PURA. Insights were gathered through 
interviews, small-group discussions, and comments on the EASE docket, producing a rich set of 
perspectives and ideas from individuals and organizations. 
Stakeholders highlighted numerous barriers and frustrations, including difficulties finding clear, 
accessible information on PURA’s website, challenges navigating PURA-regulated utility 
programs, and the high cost of participating in formal dockets. 
The consultant team documented stakeholder concerns, questions, and suggestions, 
categorizing them by type and level of engagement. A key finding was that many stakeholders 
with varying degrees of experience with PURA were moderately to very interested in “engaging, 
influencing, or participating.” However, their expectations varied widely, and the barriers they cited 
differed depending on their goals—for example, someone trying to understand how to access and 
navigate utility-run customer programs, such as the Low Income Discount Rate, faces very 
different challenges than a new advocate learning how to file testimony in a docket. 
Callout Box 2. Public Meeting #1 Feedback 
Some stakeholders do not want to know details about PURA or dockets—they only want to 
know about topics that directly affect them. Others want to directly engage, influence, or 
participate in formal PURA processes. 
At Public Meeting #1 (Appendix A), attendees were asked to rank their interest in 
participating/engaging/influencing PURA (Figure 2). Roughly 64% of respondents deeply 
desire to engage, influence, or participate in PURA (with 25% of total respondents ranking 
this as a 10). About 27% of respondents, however, noted mild-to-moderate interest in 
engaging, participating, or influencing PURA.

Barrier 1. Low public awareness and understanding of PURA 
Lack ofAwarenessofPURA’sRoleand Impact
One of the most important themes of the feedback was that many people are not aware of what 
PURA is, how PURA intersects with their lives, or the authority PURA has. Some individuals and 
organizations are interested in deepening their understanding of PURA and/or following or

Information is Inaccessible

they do not understand available information because the language is too technical, contains

Customer Insights are Not Included in Dockets 
Most who interact with and desire to engage with PURA will not participate formally in a docket. 
Most people engage with PURA, through EOE, to seek information and support on personal

insight, concerns, and challenges of those who have issues with utility services often will not be 
included in the record; these perspectives, and the trends they represent, are often absent from 
formal docket records, unless gathered and collected by an advocate participating in the dockets.

Those who may wish to be heard about an issue in a docket may not know about dockets, may 
not know which docket includes the issue they are interested in, and may not know how to find a 
specific docket or docket number. With no keyword search in the online docket system, it can be 
difficult for someone to identify dockets they are interested in and find the appropriate forum to 
share their perspectives and experiences to be considered by PURA and impact policymaking.

Recommendation 1.A. Enhance PURA informational resources. 
Connecticut residents23 need better, clearer, and more accessible information to increase their 
awareness and understanding of PURA and how PURA decisions may impact them. Although 
PURA offers some information online, it is often technical, complicated, and not presented in a 
welcoming fashion. 
This recommendation focuses on both 1) enhancing the presentation of information about PURA, 
and 2) ensuring that information is accessible to a wide range of audiences. 
Key Action: Develop and showcase more entry-level information about PURA. 
First, PURA should develop and distribute entry-level information about (1) PURA’s role in the 
regulation of utility services and (2) EOE staff’s role to respond to utility customers' questions and 
concerns and how to access them. Currently, most information about PURA is presented in an 
official and technical written form. The addition of an entry-level version of basics about PURA 
could be made available on the front page of the PURA website.24 The page should be 
understandable to new PURA stakeholders and provide explanations of important PURA

throughout the year, or as shorter videos posted on video hosting websites like YouTube. 
Key Action: Meet and go beyond ADA accessibility best practices. 
Second, PURA should strive to meet or exceed established accessibility best practices when 
developing and distributing information. The website should, at minimum, comply with American 
with Disabilities Act (ADA) website guidelines. PURA can consider whether further efforts may not

Chapter V. Implementation and Progress 
Tracking 
The preliminary assessment found that PURA has already taken several important steps to 
expand access and encourage broader regulatory participation by conducting PURA 101 
Roadshows and webinars, creating informational videos, conducting public information sessions, 
and implementing the Stakeholder Group Compensation Program. PURA remains committed to 
further expanding equity and access in its processes. 
PURA can take steps to make it easier for new and existing stakeholders to more effectively 
participate in dockets and impact outcomes. The recommended actions detailed in the 
preceding chapter can improve PURA’s decision-making by (1) improving accessibility to 
individuals that want to understand and engage with PURA, (2) creating better pathways for 
information from customers into relevant dockets, and (3) supporting new stakeholders so they 
can effectively participate in PURA proceedings. 
PURA Support in Implementation 
Successful implementation of the recommended actions will require PURA to apply a 
comprehensive lens of equity and access to its efforts. Although the recommendations provide 
guidance on actions and envisioned outcomes, PURA will need to be thoughtful and consider how 
stakeholder engagement can continue to build trust and refine the implementation process. 
PURA already envisioned needing some implementation support and included a phase to develop 
resources and provide training for staff as they transition into implementation in the consultant 
team’s scope of work. The consultant team will continue developing resources and training for 
staff after the release of this report. 
PURA has demonstrated a commitment to participate in continued education and training to 
better understand how personal experiences and perspectives can impact our ability to see and 
understand one another. Training to recognize and address unconscious biases, promote cultural 
sensitivity, and improve communication skills will only enhance implementation of the 
recommended actions. 
Implementation Plan 
PURA should adopt an implementation plan to focus its capacity and resources on priority 
recommendations. PURA will need to evaluate its own authority, capacity, and financial 
resources, as well as the desired impacts, to determine which recommendations to prioritize. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
27

STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
28 

Share Regular Updates on Implementation Progress 
Tracking Progress 
PURA currently reports quarterly and annually on regulatory activities, including: 
●
Number of dockets opened/closed.
●
Number of decisions.
●
Number of meetings, hearings or workshops, and customer complaints addressed.
through stakeholder engagement efforts.
●
Number of fines issued.
These output-based metrics help track regulatory activity, but do not capture the envisioned 
outcomes intended through the EASE docket. Success in the EASE docket will need to be 
measured over time, to understand the full impact of significant or incremental changes. It will be 
important to monitor and evaluate success of the EASE Strategy implementation over time. 
Evaluation should balance the effort required to track impacts that provide relevant and 
meaningful indicators of progress with budget, time, and resource constraints. A mix of 
qualitative and quantitative metrics can provide a comprehensive indication of progress. 
The following recommended metrics are designed to measure progress towards each of the 
three objectives. It is recommended that PURA begin tracking key metrics immediately, especially 
to capture preliminary progress and other progress relevant to the Stakeholder Group 
Compensation Program 2027 Evaluation. 
Measuring Objective 1: Increase public awareness and understanding of PURA 
and how people can engage with PURA. 
Proposed Metric: Percentage of event attendees from target communities/perspectives. 
How: At virtual or in-person events, capture attendee information through a sign-in sheet. Include 
a place to indicate representations (i.e., organization/affiliation, community, perspective48), so 
PURA can identify community/perspectives participating, and determine whether they should 
seek to increase participation from others. Each event could have an estimated percent target 
representation and PURA could track based on participants' recorded affiliations. 
Success: Ideally, this metric increases over time, especially in proceedings that most directly 
impact target community members. This quantitative metric could indicate that more 
stakeholders are successfully receiving clearer information on the website about issues and 
events, that PURA is meeting communities more where they are, and that PURA events have 
appropriate accessibility measures in place to increase access. 
48 A sign-in sheet or anonymous survey could invite participants to indicate if they represent certain 
perspectives, such as renter, low-income earner, someone with medical disabilities, person of color, or 
other underrepresented perspectives. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
29 

Proposed Metric: Website usefulness and accessibility 
How: Use website analytics to track the # of unique site visits, page visits, time on site, bounce 
rates, etc. and how the website was accessed (desktop, laptop, mobile device). PURA should 
compare website analytics pre- and post- website changes and overtime to monitor user 
experience. Pop up surveys could be an added website feature to measure visitor’s perceptions 
about the website usefulness and accessibility. 
Website analytics can help PURA track what’s happening on the website (e.g., understand visitor 
behavior, popular pages, etc.) and identify areas for improvement in terms of content and user 
experience. 
Success: Over time, PURA should expect to see website traffic increase, and user satisfaction 
increase as information evolves to meet the needs and interests of visitors. 
Proposed Metric: Participant satisfaction and understanding about PURA 
How: Conduct short exit surveys (3-5 questions) at the end of events. Questions could focus on 
the following: 
●
Were participants satisfied with the engagement?
●
Did participants gain knowledge and understanding about PURA?
●
Did participants feel they had an opportunity to contribute to the discussion?
●
How can PURA continue to engage with participants?
A simple, quick survey after each engagement will help PURA assess the efficacy of events and 
information provided to improve participant awareness levels and understanding or whether 
future events and content should be adapted. 
Success: As PURA responds and adapts events based on participant feedback, participant 
satisfaction and understanding of PURA should increase over time. 
Measuring Objective 2: Expand ways for public input to contribute to and inform 
matters before PURA. 
Proposed Metric: Number of public comments submitted successfully to a proceeding, 
through each available method 
How: Each PURA decision cites the number of public comments submitted and considered in a 
decision. The recommendations in the Strategy would allow for more public comments to make it 
into decision making, through the normal docket platform, the Executive Secretary, EOE or other 
non-decisional staff comments or briefings, and a new and more accessible public comment 
form. 
To track if and how well these new processes work, PURA should have a way to track the number 
of customer inquiries received, how they were received, what topic or issue they pertain to, and 
the percent of comments that were able to be conveyed to a docket as a public comment. 
Success: Knowing the quantity of public comments submitted and by what method they were 
submitted will give PURA data on what methods are most effective, and, ideally, show an increase 
in public engagement via public comment over time. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
30 

Measuring Objective 3: Continue increasing support to the public to participate in 
dockets in ways that will help them to influence outcomes. 
Proposed Metric: Representation and successful contribution of Stakeholder Group 
Compensation recipients 
How: For the purposes of the Stakeholder Group Compensation Program 2027 Evaluation report 
to the legislature and beyond, PURA should maintain a running database/spreadsheet to track 
key information, including but not limited to49: 
●
Stakeholder Group Compensation applicants, awardees, denials with explanations.
●
Communities represented and how representation in the program changes over time.
●
Dockets recipients participate in.
●
Compensation awarded to individual groups, in each proceeding, and in total.
●
Time to receive compensation.
●
Remaining funds available.
In addition to these qualitative metrics, it will be important for PURA to provide opportunities for 
participant qualitative feedback on the program’s effectiveness. 
Success: Data collection to track the above indicators can aid in understanding (1) gaps in 
represented communities/perspectives, (2) the breadth of issues (dockets) benefiting from 
stakeholder compensation, and (3) the depth of stakeholder impact (compensation awarded due 
to significant contribution as a proxy). 
An expansion of representation and an increase in awards of compensation will indicate that 
program changes are supporting greater docket participation and PURA decision-making. 
Proposed Metric: User experience with online docket enhancements 
How: PURA should conduct an annual survey of docket participants and intervenors to rate their 
experience and offer feedback on enhancements to the online docket process that may be 
implemented as part of the EASE Strategy. Such enhancements include new docket comment 
forms, docket summaries, and any changes to the docket system structure, navigation and other 
features meant to support accessibility. 
Success: This information will help PURA assess any new docket system activity, which is 
expected to grow over time. Moreover, understanding user experience and perceptions of docket 
system tools and resources will inform continuous improvement efforts to enhance user 
experience, increase docket participation and support decisions. Ideally, over time, survey results 
will reflect more positive feedback and less critiques; any such assessments will be qualitative. 
49 PURA is already collecting much of this data. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
31 

Reporting and Accountability 
PURA staff have made clear a desire and intention to integrate equity into PURA proceedings. 
Expanding access and equity must be initiated and sustained by PURA as an institution to enact 
meaningful and long-lasting structural change. 
The recommendations proposed are for PURA’s consideration to increase participation of 
underrepresented individuals and communities in PURA proceedings. However, the EASE 
consultant team recognizes that not all may be implemented immediately or prove feasible. As a 
future step, PURA will need to decide which to pursue and set a timeline for any implementation. 
To hold PURA accountable for carrying out the EASE Strategy, the agency should provide regular 
updates on its implementation efforts. These updates will demonstrate PURA’s commitment to 
following through with its EASE Strategy, ensure transparency and accountability, and track the 
impact. PURA could also more formally report on its progress by: 
●
Convening an EASE Implementation Working Group to support PURA’s EASE Strategy
implementation. The working group could provide support in the form of outreach and
sharing ideas and connections. Ideally, members would commit to a set of meetings or
other activities to support PURA staff, and should be compensated, perhaps through the
Stakeholder Group Compensation Program. Working Group meetings would be open to
the public, and meeting summaries would be noticed on a dedicated, well-publicized, and
accessible webpage.
●
Hosting regular updates and public meetings to share updates about the progress of
implementation with EASE stakeholders, staff, and members of the public. Regular
updates could be provided on PURA’s public facing website and/or the EASE
Implementation Working Group dedicated webpage, via press releases, at community
outreach events, public meetings, etc. Events and public meetings could allow time for
questions and discussion, and ongoing feedback.
Alternatively, PURA can explore if the Connecticut Equity and Environmental Justice Advisory 
Council (CEEJAC) would be an appropriate venue for the above updates.50 In any form, regular 
updates should include updates on progress, including status of activities (completed, in 
progress, or planned), challenges, questions encountered, lessons learned, tracking on proposed 
metrics—and movement on any longer term recommendations (as determined through PURA’s 
implementation plan). 
Facilitating an EASE Working Group and/or reporting to EASE Stakeholders and other interested 
parties is important to maintain transparency and accountability to the EASE Strategy and 
adopted implementation plan. Providing transparency will not be simple; it will require PURA staff 
time and resources to monitor, track and compile updates and present them to relevant 
audiences. 
50 CEEJAC is an advisory council to the Commissioner of Connecticut’s Department of Energy and
Environmental Protections (DEEP) on issues related to current and historic environmental injustice and 
inequities across the state. The council was established through Governor Lamont’s Executive Order 21-3, 
which was signed in 2021. CEEJAC meets quarterly and hosts subcommittee meetings and its 
membership includes the DEEP Commissioner, CT-based environmental justice community 
representatives, environmental advocacy organizations, large/small businesses and industry, municipality 
representatives, and CT’s Departments of Public Health, Economic and Community Development, Housing, 
and Transportation. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA 
32 

Chapter VI. Conclusion 
Opening the EASE Strategy docket and pursuing ways to bring a wider range of perspectives into 
PURA proceedings is commendable and essential to making decisions that address the diverse 
needs of utility users in Connecticut. The EASE Strategy was developed by examining PURA’s 
existing efforts and processes and by listening to individuals who currently engage with PURA–as 
well as those who wish to do so in the future–about their experiences. 
Three main barriers to engagement with PURA were identified: 
●
Low public awareness and understanding of PURA
●
Limited ways for public input to contribute to and inform matters before PURA
●
Significant resources are often required for participation in PURA proceedings
This EASE Strategy offers recommendations and key actions to address the barriers that were 
based on the information collected as part of the EASE proceeding, as well as best practices and 
insights from other states and organizations. The result is a comprehensive set of actions PURA 
can take to meet the EASE goal of making participation easier, more meaningful, and efficient, 
with the following objectives as a guide: 
●
Increase public awareness and understanding of PURA and how people can engage with
PURA.
●
Expand ways for public input to contribute to and inform matters before PURA.
●
Continue increasing support to the public to participate in dockets in ways that will help
them to influence outcomes.
Going forward, PURA and stakeholders will need to assess and prioritize the recommendations to 
determine any implementation next steps. A critical component will be adopting related metrics 
and reporting that offer transparent insight into PURA’s progress. This EASE Strategy captures a 
moment in time; but utility issues and the related needs of stakeholders will always be evolving. 
Establishing and maintaining ongoing relationships with communities across the state will make 
seeing and understanding these evolutions easier and more effective in the future. 
The EASE Strategy marks a milestone in PURA’s ongoing efforts to increase accessibility and 
public engagement. It places particular emphasis on including those who have not historically 
participated in decision-making processes. Implementation of this Strategy will deepen public 
participation and mutual understanding and improve how PURA serves people across the state. 
STRENGTHENING EQUITY AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AT PURA

title: PURA Final Decision — Docket 24-05-16: Application of L.C. Doane Company for Qualification of 110 Pond Meadow Road, Essex, CT as a Cass I Renewable Energy Source
text:
STATE OF CONNECTICUT 

PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY 
TEN FRANKLIN SQUARE 
NEW BRITAIN, CT 06051 

DOCKET NO. 24-05-16 
APPLICATION OF L.C. DOANE COMPANY FOR 
QUALIFICATION OF 110 POND MEADOW ROAD, 
ESSEX, CT AS A CLASS I RENEWABLE ENERGY 
SOURCE 

July 24, 2024 

By the following Commissioners: 

John W. Betkoski, III 
Michael A. Caron 
Marissa P. Gillett 

DECISION 

DECISION 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 

A. 
SUMMARY 

In this Decision, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority determines that the solar 
generation facility located at 110 Pond Meadow Road in Essex, Connecticut qualifies 
as a Class I renewable energy source. 

B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 

By Application received May 15, 2024 (Application), L.C. Doane Company 
(Company) requests that the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority) determine 
that the solar generation facility (Facility or Project) qualifies as a Class I renewable 
energy source. 

C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 

There is no statutory requirement for a hearing, no person requested a hearing, 
and none was held. 

D. 
PARTICIPANTS 

The Authority recognized the following as Participants to this proceeding: L. C. 
Doane Company, P.O. Box 700, Ivoryton, CT 06442; the Office of Consumer Counsel, 
Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, CT 06051; and the Commissioner of the Department 
of Energy and Environmental Protection, 79 Elm Street, Hartford, CT 06106. 

II. 
STANDARD REVIEW 

Pursuant to § 16-1(a)(20) of the General Statutes, “Class I renewable energy 
source” includes energy derived from solar power. 

III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 

As provided in the Application, the Facility generates electricity using solar power. 
The Project began commercial operation on December 22, 2008, and has an installed 
capacity of 0.2448 MW. The Facility's NEPOOL GIS Identification Number is NON36625. 
The Project is a behind-the-meter facility located in Connecticut and shall be subject to 
audits by the Authority. 

The Facility has been accepted into The Connecticut Light and Power Company 
d/b/a Eversource Energy’s (CL&P)’s 15-year Zero Emissions Renewable Energy Credit 
Program and its electric generation output will be tracked by a CL&P Monitoring System. 
All electricity produced by the Project will be either sold to CL&P or used at the location 
of the Facility. 

Docket No. 24-05-16 

Page 2 

IV. 
CONCLUSION 

The Authority reviewed all information in the record and finds that pursuant to 
Gen. Statutes § 16-1(a)(20), the Facility qualifies as a Class I renewable energy source, 
effective April 1, 2024. The Authority assigns the Facility Connecticut Renewable 
Portfolio Standard Registration No. CT240516. 

The Authority’s determination in this docket is based on the information 
submitted by the Company. The Authority may reverse its ruling or revoke the 
Company’s registration if any material information provided proves to be false or 
misleading. The Company is reminded that it is obligated to notify the Authority within 
10 days of any changes to any of the information it has provided.

DECISION 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) establishes the 
Customer Legal Advocacy Services Program (CLAS Program or Program), including an 
application and approval process to distribute up to $1 million annually to organizations 
or individuals providing services with the express purpose of attaining participation in 
public service company (PSC) programs that assist customers with utility bill or arrearage 
payments as contemplated in General Statutes § 16-262(b)(8), as amended by Public Act 
23-102, § 30. 

The Program will enable organizations or individuals interested in providing such 
services to apply to be included on the Program’s qualified provider list (QPL). Providers 
who meet the requirements of the program and are approved to participate as indicated 
by the QPL (Providers) would then be able to seek reimbursement according to the 
program parameters outlined herein starting on January 1, 2025. 

This docket will also serve as the administrative record for applications for the QPL, 
as well as for reimbursement submissions from eligible providers.

E. 
ALIGNMENT WITH REGULATORY OBJECTIVES 
The Authority created a framework for investigating methods for realizing an 
equitable modern electric grid in Connecticut (EMG Framework), as well as for near-term 
and long-term plans to ensure continued developments to Connecticut’s electric grid. 
Decision, Oct. 2, 2019, Docket No. 17-12-03, PURA Investigation into Distribution System 
Planning of the Electric Distribution Companies (EMG Decision). 

PURA established the following objectives for its EMG Framework: 

1. Support (or remove barriers to) the growth of Connecticut’s green economy; 
2. Enable a cost-effective, economy-wide transition to a decarbonized future; 
3. Enhance customer access to a more resilient, reliable, and secure commodity; and 
4. Advance the ongoing energy affordability dialogue in the state, particularly in 
underserved communities.

EMG Decision, p. 26. 

Additionally, the Authority established four overarching regulatory objectives to 
guide the development of a comprehensive performance-based regulation (PBR) 
framework:3 

1. Excellent Operational Performance: Achieve the highest standards for EDC 
performance in terms of efficiency, reliability, resiliency, and supply; 
2. Public Policy Achievement: Meet state-level GHG emissions, decarbonization, and 
DER deployment targets, and enhance environmental protection and equity 
measures; 
3. Customer Empowerment and Satisfaction: Beyond traditional customer 
satisfaction metrics, empower EDC customers to take greater control of their 
energy services (e.g., deploying DERs and other grid-edge technologies, reducing 
their carbon footprint, etc.) and expenditures (e.g., lowering their monthly utility 
bill); and 
4. Reasonable, Equitable, and Affordable Rates: Ensure customers across all 
socioeconomic classes receive reasonable rates and equitable access to the same 
products and services. 

Decision, Apr. 26, 2023, Docket No. 21-05-15, PURA Investigation into a Performance 
Based Regulation Framework for the Electric Distribution Companies (PBR Phase 1 
Decision), p. 13. 

The objectives outlined in the PBR Framework are rooted in and have broad 
applicability to all utility regulatory matters and, as such, are designed to guide current 
and future utility regulation in Connecticut. Id., p. 11. Further, the Authority developed 
these regulatory goals to be inclusive of the four objectives of the EMG Framework and 
legacy regulatory goals of safe, reliable, and affordable service. Id., p. 13. 

The CLAS Program directly supports EMG Framework Objective 4, as well as the 
third and fourth regulatory goals established through the PBR Phase 1 Decision. 
Specifically, the CLAS Program will provide an additional tool for underserved customers 
to access and navigate the available programs offered by PSCs and to negotiate 
reasonable amortization payment plans; thereby furthering energy affordability and 
enhancing customers’ ability to control their energy expenditures.

II. 
CLAS PROGRAM ELEMENTS 
The Authority has established or otherwise sought to improve the utilities’ 
affordability and arrearage forgiveness programs. See, e.g., Decision, Oct. 11, 2023, 
Docket No. 23-05-01, Annual Review of Affordability Program and Offerings (Energy 
Affordability Annual Review). The objective of the CLAS Program is to provide an 
augmentative resource for customers that will help to ensure that customers are able to 
access and participate in the affordability and arrearage forgiveness programs for which 
they are eligible. As discussed in multiple proceedings on these topics, increasing the 
ability of customers to pay their utility bills avoids service terminations and aims to 
decrease uncollectible expenses, which are recovered by utilities from all ratepayers. 

To further the Program objectives described in Section I.C, the Authority will 
maintain a QPL. Utility customers that call EOE seeking assistance with utility bill or 
arrearage payments, including enrolling in a payment plan or utility bill program, may be 
referred to the QPL to select a Provider to assist with the resolution of their issue at no 
cost to the customer. Providers will then provide eligible services designed to assist PSC 
customers with matters related to utility bills, arrearage payments, and service 
terminations. A referral from EOE is not required, and Customers can also seek eligible 
services directly from Providers. Providers will submit monthly invoices directly to the 
relevant PSCs for reimbursement.

A. 
ELIGIBLE SERVICES 
Services eligible for reimbursement are limited to “legal services with the express 
purpose of attaining participation in public service company programs designed to assist 
customers with utility bill or arrearage payments, including negotiating a reasonable 
amortization agreement . . . .” General Statutes § 16-262c (b)(8). Such services include, 
but are not limited to, reviewing customer documents, negotiating on behalf of a customer 
as their authorized representative, reviewing, drafting, and sending correspondence or 
otherwise communicating with a PSC on behalf of a customer, conducting legal research, 
and providing advice to customers. 

In its Written Comments, CCA provided examples of customer situations that 
would benefit from being served by the Program. CCA Comments, Apr. 19, 2024, 
Comments, pp. 2-3. CCA further provided examples of services it currently renders to 
customers that fall within the Program’s purview, including assistance in understanding 
how much a customer needs to pay under a payment arrangement, submitting verification 
of income, learning about available programs, reviewing customer bills to ensure they are 
enrolled in available programs, joining clients in calling their utility’s customer service 
representative, and assisting with next steps after service is terminated. Id. These 
examples are the type of legal services that are eligible under the Program to provide 
additional resources for customers to navigate their options presented by their utility. 
B. 
CUSTOMER ELIGIBILITY 
The CLAS Program is intended to supplement the existing resources offered by 
PSCs and to help customers that have not otherwise been able to attain meaningful 
participation in an existing affordability program. 

The Joint PSC Comments noted that the existing affordability programs are only 
for residential customers, and that they have not received a significant number of 
complaints from commercial customers. Joint PSC Comments, Apr. 19, 2024, p. 11. 
CCA supports prioritizing residential hardship customers. CCA Comments, Apr. 19, 
2024, p. 3. However, as demonstrated by the hundreds of thousands of previously 
unreached customers identified as hardship after data sharing with the Department of 
Social Services, CCA highlights that there are customers without a hardship designation 
but who qualify and may benefit from the CLAS Program. Id., p. 2. OCC supports aligning 
the participation criteria for the CLAS Program with the Stakeholder Group Compensation 
program, but does not believe that residential customer participation in the CLAS Program 
should be limited to hardship customers or customers residing in an environmental justice 
community. OCC, Apr. 19, 2024, Comments, pp. 1-2. 

The Authority finds that overly limiting Program eligibility may inadvertently exclude 
customers in need from using the resources provided. Therefore, the CLAS Program will 
reimburse Providers for providing eligible services to residential and small business utility 
customers, up to the statutory maximum of one million dollars each year. For the 
purposes of this Program, the Authority defines a small business customer as “a 
commercial or industrial electric customer with less than a two-hundred-kilowatt peak load 
that is a ‘small business’ under section 4-168a of the General Statutes.” Conn. Gen. Stat. 
§ 16-9c(a)(6). General Statutes § 4-168a(a)(2) defines “small business” as “a business

entity, including its affiliates, that (A) is independently owned and operated and (B) 
employs fewer than two hundred fifty full-time employees or has gross annual sales of 
less than five million dollars . . . .” 4 Consequently, small businesses would need to satisfy

Accordingly, Eversource, YGS, Aquarion, UI, CNG, SCG, and Connecticut Water

C. 
REQUESTS FOR PROPOSAL FROM QUALIFIED PROVIDERS 
The Authority will conduct a Request for Proposals (RFP) process using an 
application template (Application)5 to obtain information from individuals and 
organizations seeking to provide services through the CLAS Program. By prequalifying 
Providers before they offer eligible services and request reimbursement, the Authority is 
able to: (1) screen organizations and individuals for their ability to provide services; and 
(2) budget appropriately for each organization or individual within the $1 million annual 
statutory cap. Overall, a QPL will provide clarity to customers seeking assistance while 
minimizing the program’s administrative burden. 

The Application requires prospective Providers to include information about their 
organization’s services, including, but not limited to hourly billing rate, overhead and 
administrative costs, experience with utility advocacy, and language proficiency. The 
Authority will then review Applications and select Providers based on their qualifications 
and capacity to assist customers. Selected Providers will be required to assist customers 
of all seven covered PSCs, as needed. The QPL will also be publicly available on the 
Authority’s website. 

The Authority will launch the first CLAS Program RFP process in Fall of 2024 to 
select qualified Providers following the Decision’s issuance, enabling providers on the 
QPL to begin providing services on January 1, 2025. The Authority anticipates 
conducting a second RFP process in 2026 to provide an opportunity to update the 
Qualified Provider List and associated provider budget allocations based on applications 
received. Thereafter, the Authority anticipates conducting an RFP process every three 
years to allow for changes to the QPL; however, the specific timing and frequency of the 
RFPs are subject to change.

D. 
DISBURSEMENT OF FUNDS 
1. Provider Budget Allocation 
The Authority considered multiple approaches to determine budgets among 
Providers to adhere to the overall $1 million annual Program statutory cap. OCC suggests 
dividing the budget equally among all selected Providers. OCC Comments, p. 2. CCA 
recommends allocating the budget based on the geographic area served. CCA 
Comments, p. 4. However, to approve a proposed budget for each Provider, the Authority 
must first understand the number of Providers that are applying for the CLAS Program, 
as well as their qualifications and bandwidth for offering services to PSC customers. 
Therefore, as part of its review of applications submitted, the Authority will determine a 
not-to-exceed annual budget for each Provider, considering the number of service 
providers to be included on the QPL, the requested budget, and the stated capacity of 
each provider. 

Once a total maximum annual budget for each Provider is set by the Authority, 
each budget would be subsequently subdivided to reserve funds for the customers of 
each PSC. The subdivision will be made in proportion to the number of customers of 
each PSC; see Table 1 below. Importantly, these PSC allocations are not binding, but 
rather serve as a general guideline for Providers as they track incurred expenses 
throughout the year.
