Notwithstanding, customer requests for a given Provider’s services may 
necessitate adjustments to Providers’ initial budget allocations. For illustrative purposes, 
if Provider B is allocated a total annual budget of $250,000, but incurs $250,000 of eligible 
Program expenses within the first six months of a calendar year, the Authority may elect 
to allocate Provider B with additional funds from other Providers’ allocations if such funds 
have not yet been used by those Providers. As such, quarterly adjustments may be made 
to the Provider budget allocations, as needed, to re-allocate the remaining funding within 
each Provider based on year-to-date data to adjust for customer needs. This flexibility 
mechanism is intended to allow the Program to adapt to customer needs and inform the 
Authority of trends in how customers are using the Program. 
a. Advance Funding 
Some Providers may require advance funding to begin providing eligible services. 
Further, advance funding may facilitate diverse participation from Providers. In the 
Application, prospective Providers will identify the amount they require in advance funding 
to provide eligible services to customers and identify the specific start-up costs they 
consider necessary to furnish such services. Further, organizational financial statements 
will be required to demonstrate a Provider’s need for advance funding. Any advance 
funding will serve as a retainer for Providers to ensure that the eligible services are 
available to customers under the Program. Providers must return all unused portions of 
any advance funding at the end of a Program year. 

Once the Authority selects the Providers, the total amount of required advance 
funding will be allocated across all the PSCs covered under the Program, based on the 
total number of customers of each company. As the Authority cannot predict how many 
of each PSC’s customers will use the CLAS Program, the advance funding costs for the 
Program will be allocated to all covered under the Program using the proportions 
assigned in Table 1 above. The advance funding costs would later be reconciled based 
on the proportion of customers served from each company in the program year. The 
Authority may consider providing advance funding that represents less than 50% of the

Moreover, the Authority may only offer advanced funding in the first year a Provider

b.
Overhead and Administrative Costs
Overhead and administrative costs are necessary for Providers to provide eligible 
services under the CLAS Program. Such a practice is consistent with other grant 
programs for direct legal services. CCA Comments, p. 4. CCA opines that the accepted 
range of an overhead and administrative cost rate ranges from 10-25%. Id. Under the 
Program, the Authority allows the use of an overhead and administrative rate of up to 
15%. 
2.
PSC Cost Allocation
PSCs will only pay for the eligible services rendered by Providers to their 
customers under this Program. As described in Section II.D.3, the Authority will review 
data reporting submitted by Providers to verify that the PSCs are charged only for services 
provided to their own customers. Quarterly adjustments to the allocations to each PSC 
within each Provider’s approved annual budget may be necessary, as described in 
Section II.D.1. 
3.
Invoicing
Providers are required to submit monthly invoices directly to the relevant PSCs for 
reimbursement by utilizing the Template Invoice provided in Appendix B. The applicable 
PSC will reimburse the Provider for the eligible services provided to the companies’ 
customers, as well as make any advanced payments deemed necessary by the Authority 
in its review of Provider Applications. Payments must be rendered within 45 days of 
receipt of an invoice. 
In addition, on a quarterly basis, each Provider is required to submit a report as 
compliance in this docket that indicates: 
•
The total invoiced amount for that quarter, broken out by PSC;
•
Number of customers served, broken out by PSC and by town;
•
Number of customers served, broken out by affordability program participation
(e.g. Low-Income Discount Rate, Matching Payment Program, flexible payment
plan, etc.);
•
The total number of hours billed by PSC; and
•
The total amount expected to be invoiced in the following month.
Each Provider’s quarterly report will be reviewed to determine whether and how 
funds should be reallocated to each Provider, as discussed in Section II.D.1. The 
Authority will subsequently notify the Providers of any reallocations within 21 calendar 
days of receiving the quarterly reports. This review is intended to maintain flexibility of 
the CLAS Program to accommodate requests for eligible services from customers to each 
Provider.

PROVIDER ANNUAL REPORTING REQUIREMENTS
Providers are required to submit an annual report to the Authority by February 1 of
the following year6 that includes a summary of the quarterly report information for the 
entire previous calendar year, and additional data regarding the customers they assisted 
in attaining participation in a PSC’s payment arrangement or arrearage program; see 
Appendix C; Appendix D. Specifically, the annual reports shall include anonymized client 
data, including the town of each customer helped, the associated utility, the household 
income range, and a narrative describing trends. The service Providers are directed to 
file annual reports as compliance in the instant proceeding. 
The Authority may conduct annual review proceeding(s) to assess whether 
modifications are required to ensure the CLAS Program is providing equitable, statewide 
service, is efficiently serving customers, and is implemented efficiently by Providers.

and may seek recovery of such deferred costs in their next rate case. Carrying charges

DECISION 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
In this Decision, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA or Authority) 
considers the implementation of the provisions of Public Act No. 23-199 (PA 23-199 or 
the Act).1 The Decision also discusses the processes and procedures related to the 
transfer of gas and electric service from a commercial tenant to the commercial tenant’s 
landlord when a commercial tenant is at risk of service termination for nonpayment of gas 
and electric bills. The Authority prescribes herein the form to be used by gas and electric 
service companies to accomplish the goals of this Act and presents its directives for the 
implementation of the provisions contained within the Act. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
PA 23-199 was passed by the General Assembly in June 2023 and signed into law 
by Governor Lamont on June 29, 2023. The Act is expected to enable landlords to protect 
leased properties from damages caused by the termination of utility services and is 
intended to alleviate some of the recent economic challenges affecting the state’s 
property owners. See Energy and Technology Committee, Joint Favorable Report 
(Report), March 14, 2023, p. 1. 
Section 2(b) of PA 23-199 required that the Authority initiate an uncontested 
proceeding to implement a process to notify certain property owners of pending utility 
service terminations. Pursuant to the Act, each gas company and electric distribution 
company, i.e., The Connecticut Light and Power Company and Yankee Gas Services 
Company, each individually d/b/a Eversource Energy (CL&P and Yankee, respectively; 
jointly Eversource), The United Illuminating Company, Connecticut Natural Gas 
Corporation and The Southern Connecticut Gas Company (UI, CNG, and SCG 
respectively; collectively Avangrid) (collectively with Eversource, Companies) will now be 
subject to certain notification requirements. Beginning no later than January 1, 2024, the 
Companies shall provide notice of service termination, via U.S. Mail, not less than 72-
hours prior to the termination of said service to a person or requestor who certifies that 
they are the owner of a property that is used exclusively for nonresidential purposes and 
said property does not contain more than 12,000 square feet of total floor area to which 
the Companies provide service that is billed to a customer other than the person or 
requestor. 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
The Authority established this proceeding by Notice of Proceeding on July 27, 
2023. The Authority used this docket to establish the processes and procedures related 
to the transfer of gas and electric service from a commercial tenant to the commercial 
tenant’s landlord when a commercial tenant is at risk of service termination for 
nonpayment of gas and electric bills. 

1 See Appendix A. 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 2 

The Authority issued a Notice of Request for Written Comments on July 28, 2023, 
and requested that Participants discuss implementation concerns and parameters of PA 
23-199 and submit those responses no later than August 16, 2023. 
The Authority issued interrogatories on August 17, 2023, and conducted a 
technical meeting on October 10, 2023, to discuss Participants’ responses to 
interrogatories and written comments submitted in this proceeding. The technical 
meeting was held via remote access. Following the technical meeting, the Participants 
submitted late filed exhibits. 
The Authority issued a proposed final Decision on November 20, 2023, and offered 
Participants the opportunity to submit written responses. 
D. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS OR PARTICIPANTS 

The Authority recognized Eversource, UI, CNG, SCG, Yankee, the Office of 
Consumer Counsel (OCC), the Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement (EOE), 
and the Commissioner of the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection 
(DEEP) as Participants to this proceeding. The Authority also recognized the Center for 
Children’s Advocacy and Connecticut Legal Services as Interested Persons. 
II. 
PUBLIC ACT 23-199 
A. 
ACT REQUIREMENTS 
Public Act 23-199 requires that each gas and electric company, as defined in 
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-1, notify property owners of potential termination of service under 
certain defined circumstances. Specifically, the Act requires that: 
(1) upon request of a person (Requestor) who certifies that they are the owner of 
a property that is used exclusively for nonresidential purposes and contains not 
more than twelve thousand square feet of total floor area that is rented or 
leased 
(2) each gas company and electric distribution company shall notify such 
Requestor by United States mail not less than seventy-two hours prior to 
terminating service to such property. 
The Act further requires the gas and electric companies to: 
(1) reinstate gas or electric service by reverting such service to the Requestor's 
name, if, at a later date, the Requestor asks for reinstatement, if 
(2) the Requestor is not the customer of record, and 
(3) provided that the request is made in writing in a form prescribed by PURA. 
The Act further provides that no gas or electric company may disclose to the 
Requestor the reason why the company is terminating the service and that the Act shall 
not be construed to require the Requestor to pay an account balance or arrearage left by 
the customer. Additionally, the Requestor is responsible for notifying the electric or gas 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 3 

company in a timely manner of any change to their mailing address or of the sale of such 
property. PA 23-199(2)(c)-(d). 
B. 
PRESCRIBED FORM 
PA 23-199 directed the Authority to create the form that will be used by property 
owners/landlords requesting notification of a service termination. Pursuant to the Act, the 
form must include: 
(1) A certification that the requestor is the owner of the property that is the subject 
of the request; and 
(2) the mailing address of the requestor that shall be used by such gas or electric 
distribution company, as applicable, to mail notice in accordance with subdivision 
(1) of subsection (a) of this section. 
PA 23-199(2)(b). 
III. 
IMPLEMENTATION ISSUES 
A. 
COMPANY RESPONSES 
1. Avangrid 
The Avangrid companies presented a number of practical concerns with PA 23-
199. Chiefly, the Avangrid companies are concerned over the requirement for a notice, 
delivered via U.S. Mail, no later than 72-hours prior to a service termination. Avangrid 
Comments, p. 1. The Avangrid companies stated that a minimum of six days (or 144 
hours) would be needed in order to meet the postal service requirement. Id. Any delays 
in the delivery of a mailed notice could impact potential situations where the companies 
might be unable to access their equipment while awaiting the delivery of the termination 
notice. Id. The Avangrid companies noted that it was unclear whether PA 23-199’s 
requirements could result in a customer having to delay a move out request as well as 
identifying which party would be responsible for the bill during the 72-hour waiting period. 
Id. 
Another area of concern was the verification/identification of the property owner 
and validation of the square footage of a given property. In this regard, the Avangrid 
companies insisted that the Companies cannot and should not be responsible for 
evaluating or otherwise validating property ownership or a property’s floor area. Id. 
On the subject of implementation of the provisions of PA 23-199, the Avangrid 
companies expect that a number of internal processes will need to be built into its 
systems. These processes include the automation of the form letter issued to persons 
requesting the termination notification, the database to store the requestor’s records, and 
the automation of letters to be issued when there is a pending disconnect. Id., p. 2. 
2. Eversource 
Eversource raised initial concerns with the U.S. Mail service requirement 
component. Eversource stated that in cases where the termination of service is based 
upon a non-payment issue, there should be no significant impact and the appropriate 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 4 

notice would be accomplished through an IT change. Eversource Comments, p. 3. 
Because Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100(d)(1)(A) mandates that no utility company 
shall terminate service to a customer prior to 13 days after notice of the proposed 
termination has been sent via first class mail to the address of the customer, 72-hour 
notice to a landlord can be accomplished during that 13-day timeframe. Id. 
However, with the mail service requirement for the notice in situations where the 
customer is moving out or voluntarily ending service, Eversource stated that it may be 
necessary to delay the effective date of the termination. This delay would be needed to 
comply with the requirement of the termination notice provided, via U.S. Mail, with at least 
72 hours prior notice. Id., p. 3. Eversource also raised concerns regarding interpretation 
of the term “requestor” and what party is responsible for the cost of the service during the 
72-hour notice period. Id., p. 4. Eversource took the position that the cost for service 
would remain with the tenant until such time as the landlord makes the proper request, in 
accordance with the Act, at which time it would transfer to the landlord as the Requestor. 
IV. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
TERMINATION TYPES 
Any notice of a service termination provided to a person or entity requesting said 
notice under the provisions of PA 23-199 must be issued via U.S. Mail not less than 72-
hours prior to the termination of such service. This requirement presents certain hurdles 
that must be addressed to ensure the Companies’ compliance. 
Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100(15) defines “termination” or “terminate” to mean 
“the voluntary discontinuance of service to an individual utility customer but shall not 
include interruption or curtailment of service consistent with interruption pursuant to 
[PURA]-approved tariffs or resulting from forced outages, energy or capacity shortages 
or other emergencies.” For the purposes of PA 23-199, there are two types of service 
termination. The first type of service termination occurs when a customer has been 
issued a termination notice under the provisions contained within Conn. Agencies Regs. 
§ 16-3-100. The second type of termination is when the customer chooses to voluntarily 
end service such as when they are moving or simply ending their utility service with the 
company. The Companies agree that the intent of PA 23-199 is to provide notice of 
termination in both cases. Tech Mt’g Tr., Oct. 10, 2023, 14:13-17 – 15:1-4. 
1. Termination in Accordance with Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100 
Service terminations pursuant to Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100 involve specific 
regulatory requirements that must be met. Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100(d)(1)(A) 
requires that no utility company shall terminate service to a customer prior to 13 days 
after notice of the proposed termination has been sent via first class mail to the address 
of the customer. 
The Avangrid companies stated that in order to meet the requirements of PA 23-
199, it would require no less than seven business days prior to the disconnection date to 
allow for reasonable delivery time. Avangrid Interrog. Resp. PURA-8. Eversource stated 
that its timeframe for ensuring the delivery of a mailed notice is ten days, or seven 
business days. Tr., 8:14-17. Given that the notice of termination to a customer must be 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 5 

provided with 13 days’ notice, the Companies were asked if the PA 23-199 notice 
requirement could be met if said notice were mailed at the same time as the customer’s 
termination notice. Avangrid stated that it would need to reprogram its customer 
information system, but it would be able to issue the two notices at the same time. Tr., 
7:25-8:3. Avangrid also noted that by issuing both notices at the same time, it would be 
able to comply with the mail service provisions of PA 23-199. Tr., 9:22-0:8. Eversource 
too was confident that it would be able to comply with the mail service requirements of 
PA 23-199 if said notice was issued simultaneously with a customer’s termination notice. 
Tr., 9:10-10:5. Based upon this information, the Authority finds that in cases where a 
customer termination is provided pursuant to the provisions of Conn. Agencies Regs. § 
16-3-100, the mail service requirements of PA 23-199 will be met if both notices are 
issued at the same time. 
Accordingly, the Companies are ordered to revise their internal processes so that 
when a customer termination notice is issued pursuant to Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-
100, the notice required under PA 23-199 shall be issued simultaneously. 
2. Termination Upon Customer Request 
The second type of termination, the customer-requested service cancellation or 
move-out, presents a numerically larger challenge. Data provided by Avangrid, shown 
below in Table 1, indicated that terminations for service cancellation/move-out requests 
outnumbered those for delinquent balances: 

Table 1 - Avangrid Move-Out vs. Non-Payment 

Move-out Non-Payment 
2020

Avangrid Interrog. Resp. PURA-9. 

According to Avangrid, the trend in service cancellations/move-outs continued into 
2023. Tr., 10:20. To compound this issue further, the Avangrid companies often receive 
very little advance warning of a cancellation or move-out. In some cases, the first time 
the Avangrid companies find out about a customer’s cancellation is when a new customer 
calls in to establish service at the previous customer’s service address. Tr., 11:1-15. 
Without specific data to draw upon, the Avangrid companies generally believe that the 
amount of time that customers provide ahead of a service cancellation is less than ten 
days. Tr., 16:23-25. 

The data provided by Eversource, shown below in, aligned with that submitted by 
Avangrid, in that the number of terminations due to service cancellations outnumbered 
terminations for non-payment: 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 6 

Table 2 - Eversource Move-Out vs. Non-Payment 

Move-Out Non-payment 
2020 
6,473

2021

Eversource, Late Filed Ex. 1. 

While Eversource does not track the lead time that its customers provide when 
customers voluntarily cancel service, the Company commented that its customers do not 
necessarily offer advanced notice of these activities. Tr., 12:23-13:4. Similar to the 
Avangrid companies, Eversource did not have data on customer lead-time to draw upon. 
However, Eversource stated that its customers generally provided less than ten days’ 
notice of a service cancellation. Tr., 15:16-19. 
The customer-driven voluntary service cancellation, presents the Companies with 
a shared concern: which party will be billed for service from the date a customer cancels 
their service to the date upon which the mailed notice of termination is delivered to the 
Requestor? As stated above, the Companies expect mailed termination notices to arrive 
in ten days and the service cancellation or move-out occurs with generally less than ten 
days’ notice. 
Eversource intends to honor the customer’s request to cancel service but sees 
conflict between honoring the customer’s request and complying with the mail service 
requirements of PA 23-199. Tr., 20:6-13. Eversource’s understanding of the intent of PA 
23-199 is that the utility service shall remain on until that requestor receives the 
termination notice. Tr., 20:19. Avangrid agreed with Eversource that the intent of PA 23-
199 is to keep the utility service on until the requestor received the notice and echoed 
Eversource’s concern as to who will be the responsible party for the usage and 
consumption during the time period between cancellation and notice delivery. Tr., 21:1-
10. 
The Authority recognizes that the mail service requirements of PA 23-199 and its 
intent to keep the service active are coupled with the unpredictable nature of the service 
cancellation/move-out requests. The Authority acknowledges that the previously 
discussed directive of mailing both termination notices simultaneously in cases where 
service is terminated in conjunction with a Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100 termination 
is impractical in cases of voluntary service cancellation. The plan of simultaneous notice 
mailings will not alleviate the Companies’ concerns as they pertain to the service 
cancellation/move-out, which, as demonstrated by Table 1 and 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 7 

Table 2, occur more frequently. Accordingly, other measures will need to be 
implemented to meld the requirements of PA 23-199 with operational complexities of the 
service cancellation/move-out, specifically as it applies to billing the appropriate party for 
any usage during the time period between the cancellation and the delivery of the 
termination notice. 
B. 
OWNER ALLOCATION PROCESS/LANDLORD AGREEMENT PROCESS 
As part of its review and investigation into how the provisions contained in PA 23-
199 will be incorporated into the day-to-day activities of the Companies, the Authority 
sought information on existing business practices. Specifically, the Authority requested 
information on whether the Companies had procedures in place already that are similar 
to the process outlined in PA 23-199. 
1. Avangrid – Owner Allocation Process 
Avangrid identified a process it uses to identify landlords/property owners and 
associate them with an account for the purpose of reverting service to said property 
owner’s name in the event of a customer move-out. Avangrid Interrog. Resp. PURA-1. 
Avangrid refers to this process as the Owner Allocation Process (OAP). Id. The OAP 
requires that landlords provide information such as their name, mailing address, property 
address, and a signature. Avangrid stated that for the OAP to fully comply with the 
requirements of PA 23-199, several modifications and programming changes would need 
to be made to its existing customer information system. Id. To comply, Avangrid would 
require an attestation of the property’s square footage and proof of ownership. Id. 
Presently, the OAP is a voluntary process for landlords/property owners. Tr., 
38:17-18. When an account is not associated with the OAP process and Avangrid 
receives a move-out request, Avangrid’s practice is to take the service out of that 
customer’s name and issue a final bill. Tr., 28-16-23. The service would then not be in 
anyone’s name and, depending on the type of service (gas or electric), may or may not 
remain active. For electric customers, the service would not be active. Tr., 28:16-29:4. 
For gas customers, the service would remain active, but Avangrid monitors usage. Tr., 
29:4-9. Absent OAP, Avangrid does not have a specific set of procedures to follow in the 
event of a service cancellation other than the issuance of a final bill as discussed above. 
Tr., 30:1-9. 
2. Eversource – Multiple Processes 
Eversource identified three internal processes that share some similarities to the 
requirements of PA 23-199: Shut-off For Non-Payment Situation, the Third-Party 
Notification process (known as Safety Net), and the Landlord Agreement process. 
Eversource Interrog. Resp. PURA-1. The Shut-off for Non-Payment process allows for 
the notification of disconnection due to non-payment to residential and commercial 
customers following the requirements of Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100. Id. The 
Third-Party Notification process, available to residential and commercial customers, 
allows for a customer to designate a third party to receive reminder notices of past-due 
bills, cancellations of electric supplier services, or notices of service disconnection. Id. 
This process allows the third-party designee the option of making a payment or 
transferring service into their name. Id. The Landlord Agreement Process (LAP) allows 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 8 

any residential or commercial landlord to enroll and gives the landlord two options for 
periods in between tenants: (1) disconnection or (2) reversion to the landlord’s name. Id. 
LAP is a voluntary program. Tr., 33:17-21. Under LAP, if a landlord chooses the 
transfer option, the service will automatically revert into the landlord’s name when a tenant 
requests to end service such as through a move-out order. Tr. 32:20-33:16. When an 
account is not subject to the LAP, upon receipt of a move-out request, an order is 
automatically generated to disconnect the service for both electric and gas services. Tr., 
30:18-31:15. 
C. 
72-HOUR NOTIFICATION 
In Section IV.A.2, Termination Upon Customer Request, a potential billing issue 
was identified for customers who choose to voluntarily cancel service but do not provide 
the Companies with sufficient time to issue the required PA 23-199 notice. Unfortunately, 
the language of PA 23-199 does not specifically contemplate the operational complexities 
in relation to billing that is presented when a customer chooses to voluntarily end service 
where little to no notice is provided to the Companies. The customer has a full expectation 
that their utility service will end on the date of their choosing, and accordingly, will be the 
end of their billing responsibility. Under the provisions of PA 23-199, that utility service 
must remain active until 72 hours after the notice to the Requestor. Therefore, a delay 
has been created between the requested service cancellation date and the date of the 
scheduled termination by the Act’s requirement to issue the termination notice via U.S. 
Mail. It is during this delay that usage can theoretically be incurred and to which the Act 
is silent as to who is the responsible billing party. It is this billing concern that the Authority 
must address. 
As previously discussed, the Companies interpret the intent of PA 23-199 to keep 
utility service active until the Requestor has been provided the notice of termination under 
the Act. The Authority concurs with the Companies’ interpretation and believes that the 
purpose of PA 23-199 is to ensure that utility service remains active until 72 hours after 
notice of a service termination is received by the Requestor, i.e., the property owner or 
landlord. To alleviate this potential billing issue related to customers who voluntarily 
cancel their service, the Authority needs to establish a process by which not only the 
requirements of PA 23-199 can be met, but also represents an equitable solution for the 
Companies and customers. 
One interpretation of the Act is that the service remains in the tenant’s name until 
the notification to the Requestor has been accomplished. Under this interpretation, the 
Companies would be required to inform customers calling to cancel service that there 
would be a delay until the Requestor has received proper notice. None of the Companies 
have experienced conversations with customers cancelling service where said customer 
was instructed that they would need to delay the move-out date. Tr., 43:9-22, 44:10-22. 
Avangrid noted that this type of discussion could result in an adversarial conversation 
with the customer depending upon any potential bill amount if the cancellation date were 
to be delayed. Tr., 42:16-19. The Act does not explicitly authorize the Companies to 
continue billing the customer after the customer has requested their service be terminated 
on a date certain. 

Docket No. 23-07-02 

Page 9 

To that end, the Authority examined whether the OAP and LAP would be a practical 
means by which to resolve this issue. The Authority questioned the Companies on the 
feasibility of conditioning the process on the landlord’s enrollment into either OAP or LAP, 
wherein the property owner/landlord agrees to assume responsibility for usage incurred 
from the cancellation date. Eversource Interrog. Resp. PURA-1; Avangrid Interrog. Resp. 
PURA-1. 
Eversource stated that enrollment into LAP can be accomplished by the property 
owner/landlord making a request over the telephone. Tr., 33:3-5. Eversource did not see 
any additional complexity added to the PA 23-199 process if the LAP was combined with 
it as the Company did not believe that any additional information would be needed to 
meet the requirements of the Act. Tr., 45:24-46:17. Avangrid stated that the process to 
enroll into OAP is generally done with a form, via email, or U.S. Mail. Tr., 47:1-2. For the 
enrollment process, Avangrid collects a number of data points such as the name, 
address, mailing address, and phone number, in addition to getting a signature from the 
enrollee. Tr., 47:1-7. Avangrid stated that it did not foresee any added complexities with 
combining the OAP with enrollment into the notification process within PA 23-199. Tr., 
47:13. 
The Companies were queried as to the implementation of a procedure wherein the 
requestor of the notification of a utility service termination under the Act was mandated to 
assume responsibility of the utility service in the event of a customer move-out. 
Eversource stated that if this procedure was to be a requirement, it would help to alleviate 
its concerns as to the responsible billing party. Tr., 45:5-10. Avangrid stated that if the 
Requestor were to be the responsible billing party in the event of a service 
cancellation/move-out, it would clarify who is financially responsible for any usage during 
the delay period. Tr., 47:25-48:1. The Authority notes that usage should be minimal 
where there is no tenant. 
V. 
IMPLEMENTATION 
To aid in the administration of the goals of PA 23-199, the Authority orders the 
Companies to offer to enroll any Requestor, as defined in the Act, into their respective 
OAP or LAP with reversion programs. Both the OAP and LAP with reversion allow for 
service to be automatically transferred from the tenant to the property owner upon a 
customer-requested move-out event and obviates the need for termination of the service 
in that circumstance. At the time of enrolling, Requestors shall be instructed that they will 
be the responsible billing party for any usage generated on the account from the date of 
the service cancellation/move-out until the date a new customer establishes service at 
the subject service address. The OAP and the LAP with reversion accomplish the 
General Assembly’s goal of preventing damage caused by service disconnections without 
notice to property owners. 
The Authority orders the Companies to undertake the following steps to ensure 
compliance with the provisions of PA 23-199: 
(1) For termination events created by the issuance of a customer termination notice 
pursuant to the provisions of Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-3-100, the Companies 
shall issue the PA 23-199 notice simultaneously with said customer termination

notice if the Companies have received a completed Public Act 23-199 Termination

(2) For termination events created by a customer-requested service cancellation or a 
customer move-out for service addresses that do not have OAP or LAP with 
reversion in place, if the Companies have received a completed Public Act 23-199 
Termination Request Form from the eligible property owner, when the Companies 
have not been informed of a new customer at the subject service address, the 
Companies shall issue the PA 23-199 notice immediately upon knowledge of the 
termination event. 
(3) For service addresses that do not have OAP or LAP with reversion in place, if the 
Companies have received a completed Public Act 23-199 Termination Request 
Form from the eligible property owner, the PA 23-199 notice of termination shall 
include a statement that the customer at the service location requested termination 
on a date specified and that all usage at that service location shall be the 
responsibility of the Requestor from the date specified through the end of the 72-
hour notice period. 
(4) In the event of a termination created by a customer-requested service cancellation 
or a customer move-out, for service addresses that do not have OAP or LAP with 
reversion in place, the Companies shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that 
service to said location/meter remains active to satisfy the requirements of PA 23-
199 until the Requester has received 72 hours’ notice, which includes the length 
of time the Company determines necessary to allow sufficient time for notice to be 
received by the Requestor, and may be longer than 72-hours. It is the Companies’ 
responsibility to ensure that the 72 hours’ notice is satisfied prior to any termination 
of service. This order is applicable if the Companies have received a completed 
Public Act 23-199 Termination Request Form from the eligible property owner. 
(5) For termination events created by customer-requested service cancellation or a 
customer move-out when the Companies have actual knowledge of a new 
customer initiating service immediately at the subject service address, the 
Companies are not required to issue the PA 23-199 notice of termination because

(6) At the time of the initiation of any new non-residential service by an owner of the

and shall provide property owners with the information necessary to enroll in both 
the PA 23-199 notification program and the OAP or LAP with reversion. 
In its Written Exception, Avangrid requested additional implementation time to 
allow it to comply with the Act using an automated process. While the Authority 
acknowledges Avangrid’s request and the short implementation timeline, the Act is written

telephone call or online. Eversource Interrog. Resp. PURA-3. A new service

footage of a property. Eversource recommended that the square footage information 
should be self-certified by the property owner that is requesting the termination notification

The Authority also included a Termination Notice, as Appendix C, as a guide to the

While PA 23-199 only requires delivery of the notification of termination by U.S. 
Mail, the Authority sought information from the Companies regarding the use of electronic 
communications. The Companies indicated that if the Authority were to require an email 
communication component to the PA 23-199 process, they would be able to comply. The 
Companies stated that if required, an email notice could be issued to supplement the 
written notice provided that the Companies had a valid email address to use. Tr., 17:7-9

electronic communications, the Authority will not mandate this aspect into the 
implementation of the Act at this time. The Companies are free to decide if the use of 
electronic communications in the administration of termination notifications for PA 23-199 
is to their own best interest.

DECISION 

DECISION 

In the months of April and May, 2023, the following applicants (Applicants) applied 
to the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority) for an Electric Aggregator Certificate 
of Registration: New England Preferred Energy, LLC; Energy Analysis Group LLC; AEC 
Energy LLC; Summit Energy Services, Inc.; Evolution Energy Partners LLC; Cost Control 
Associates, Inc.; Taurus Advisory Group LLC; Lower Watt LLC; Balanced Rock Energy, 
Inc.; All Source Energy, LLC; The Energy Alliance LLC; Meretz Energy Group, LLC; 
Prudential Energy Services Corp.; StoneX Financial Inc.; and Burton Energy Group, LLC. 
The Authority, including its Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement (EOE), 
reviewed all of the information in the record of the above-referenced dockets pursuant to 
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245(l) and finds that the Applicants have satisfied the application 
requirements. The Authority grants each of the Applicants an Electric Aggregator 
Certificate of Registration to serve the non-residential markets requested by each 
Applicant, subject to the conditions described herein. 

Pursuant to statute and the Authority’s clarification in the March 30, 2023, Motion 
No. 16 Ruling (Motion No. 16 Ruling) in Docket No. 14-07-20RE01, PURA Development 
and Implementation of Marketing Standards and Sales Practices by Electric Suppliers - 
Revised Standards, an entity that represents the customer in securing a supplier contract 
and is ultimately compensated by the customer with the customer’s knowledge is an 
aggregator. An aggregator is the customer’s agent. If an entity represents the supplier 
in the transaction, then the entity is the agent of the supplier and the supplier must claim 
the entity on its Form 6. See Conn. Agencies Reg. § 16-245o(h)(1).1 No entity may be 
both an aggregator and an agent of suppliers. 

A review of the contracts between each Applicant and suppliers reveals that many 
of the contracts do not clearly delineate the Applicant as representing the customer and 
being compensated ultimately by the customer.2 As EOE noted in Motion No. 16 in 
Docket No. 14-07-20RE01, there may be instances in which non-residential customers 
wish to receive one bill for all of their energy supply services. In those instances, it 
benefits the non-residential customer for the supplier to include the aggregator’s 
compensation in that bill and pass that compensation straight to the aggregator. Not all 
supplier contracts provided by the Applicants, however, contain straight pass-through 
provisions. Many contain provisions in which a portion of the aggregator’s mark-up goes 
to the supplier. Others contain provisions in which the supplier pays the aggregator a flat 
fee for each customer procured, in the same way a supplier would pay an agent. Still 
others contain provisions in which the supplier pays the aggregator an amount up front, 
includes the aggregator’s mark-up in the customer’s rate, and then the supplier retains 
any excess, or that do not remove the mark-up if the customer ceases doing business 

1 Conn. Agencies Reg. § 16-245o(h)(1) provides in part that “[a]ny third-party who contracts with or is 
otherwise compensated by an electric supplier to sell electric generation services, or contracts with or is 
compensated by a third-party marketer of the electric supplier to sell electric generation services for the 
electric supplier, shall be a legal agent of the electric supplier.” 
2 StoneX Financial Inc. indicated repeatedly that it does not have contracts with suppliers even though it is 
paid by some suppliers as a pass-through. To the extent that StoneX enters into contracts with suppliers 
in the future, its contracts must abide by this Decision. 

2 

with the aggregator. Any compensation structure in which the supplier is retaining a 
portion of the aggregator’s compensation or paying the aggregator separate from the 
customer’s usage calls into question the relationship between the supplier and the 
aggregator, and between the aggregator and the customer. 

A straight pass-through is a simple concept as explained by EOE in Motion No. 16 
in Docket No. 14-07-20RE01. If the supplier’s rate is 10 cents/kWh, and the aggregator 
adds 1 cent as commission, the supplier charges the customer 11 cents/kWh and passes 
through the extra 1 cent/kWh to the aggregator. Any agreement more complicated than 
this is not a straight pass through and will not be approved by the Authority. As a result, 
the Authority directs all Applicants to revise all contracts with suppliers that currently do 
not contain simple, straightforward, pass-through compensation as described and to 
submit such revised contracts to the Authority. Any other form of compensation passed 
from a supplier to an aggregator is impermissible. 

Further, many of the current contracts between suppliers and the Applicants 
contain other provisions that call into question the Applicant’s role as the customer’s agent 
and not the agent of the supplier. For example, there are contractual provisions 
specifically stating that the supplier appoints the Applicant as a “sales representative . . . 
to promote, market, and sell” the supplier’s product. Entities that represent a customer 
do not promote, market, or sell for suppliers. Contracts say that the Applicant agrees to 
“solicit potential customers.” Again, entities that represent a customer are not permitted 
to solicit on behalf of a supplier. Contracts say that Applicants will use the supplier’s 
marketing material; however, the Applicants should not be marketing for the suppliers at 
all. In short, all contracts between the Applicants and suppliers should address only the 
Applicant’s ability to collect the straight pass-through compensation from the supplier. 
Any contract with provisions implying or calling into question the Applicant’s role and 
function as the customer’s agent must be revised to remove such provisions as a 
condition of receipt of an Electric Aggregator Certificate of Registration. 

Importantly, suppliers may not insert a provision in a contract stating that the 
Applicant is not the supplier’s agent, then have provisions throughout the contract in 
which the Applicant is treated as a supplier’s agent. Suppliers and the Applicants must 
decide if the Applicants are suppliers’ agents or if the Applicants represent customers. 
To the extent they determine the latter, their contracts must reflect that relationship. 
Equally important, Applicants must ensure that their customers understand the service 
they are performing and the costs for that service. Many Applicants indicated that they 
do not divulge their commission to their customers. The regulatory imperative in 
Connecticut supports the principle of transparency, such that customers are entitled to 
information adequately informing them that they are paying the Applicant for a service 
and that such payment is included in their supplier’s rate. Many Applicants also indicate 
that they do not divulge to customers the number of suppliers with which they do business. 
To make an informed decision, customers need to understand if an Applicant is evaluating 
bids from five suppliers or two. Customers further need to understand how the Applicant 
is selecting the bids to show to the customer (presuming it does not show the customer 
all bids). 

3 

To facilitate the requisite transparency with customers, every Applicant must 
provide each customer with three documents (Three Customer Communications).3 The 
Applicant must provide the first document at the outset of the relationship between the 
Applicant and the customer, and the document must:4 

1. Describe in detail how the Applicant will be compensated; 
2. Explain the process that the Applicant uses to find prospective rates for the 
customer; 
3. Explain to the customer the number of suppliers (or range of number) from 
which the Applicant will solicit rates and the current suppliers from whom it 
solicits;5 and 
4. Require the customer’s signature to permit the Applicant to obtain pricing for 
the customer. 

The Applicant must provide the second document to the customer once the 
Applicant has obtained prospective rates, and the document must: 

1. Tell the customer each supplier from whom the Applicant solicited prospective 
rates; 
2. Tell the customer the rates offered by each supplier; 
3. Describe the Applicant’s commission included in each rate;6 and 
4. Require the customer’s signature acknowledging receipt of said information. 

The third document is the notice required by Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-245-3(d),7 
and the Applicant would provide this notice to the customer after the customer contracted 

3 The documents referred to in this section may be electronic documents. 
4 Based on the content of this document and its timing, it is difficult to imagine the situation in which an 
Applicant may satisfy this requirement when “cold calling” potential customers. A “cold call” would have 
to result in a multi-step process in which the Applicant interacted with the customer, provided the 
document, obtained the customer’s signature, and then solicited bids for the customer. 
5 A few Applicants entered into contracts with customers that provided much of this information. If any 
Applicant believes its current customer contract complies with the requirements herein, it may continue 
to use its contract following the compliance filings addressed in Order No. 6 of this Decision. 
6 For example, if the aggregator provides rates from Supplier A and Supplier B, but the aggregator’s 
commission with Supplier A is one cent and with Supplier B is two cents, this must be explained to the 
customer. This information can be included as part of the bid package given to the customer and may 
include the Applicant’s recommendation. If the Applicant directly charges the customer a flat fee (i.e., 
does not collect a fee through the supplier) and does not include a commission and/or mark-up to the 
suppliers’ rates, it may include only the supplier’s rates, but the Applicant would be required to disclose 
the flat fee in the first document. To address changes in the market, an Applicant may seek to adjust 
their fee after the second of the Three Customer Communications have been supplied to the customer. 
An Applicant may only reduce their fee to address market conditions without additional notification to the 
customer. If an Applicant seeks to increase their fees to address market conditions, the increased fee 
must be disclosed in an updated/new offer to the customer. 
7 Conn. Agencies Reg. § 16-245-3(d) provides in part that “[n]ot more than sixty days (60) after an 
aggregated customer contracts with an electric supplier, and not more than sixty days after any renewal, 
extension or modification of such contract, the electric aggregator shall issue to the aggregated customer 

4 

with a supplier. Each Applicant shall retain the Three Customer Communications for 
three years from the date on which they are signed by the customer, as applicable. 

All Applicants must solicit prospective rates for each customer from more than one 
supplier, except in the following two limited circumstances: 

1. when an existing customer explicitly requests that an Applicant only provide 
pricing from a single supplier, and 
2. when the pricing being sought is to amend and/or extend an existing agreement 
between the customer and a particular supplier. 

Apart from these two exceptions, an entity that fails to solicit rate offers from more 
than one supplier and enrolls customers with that supplier will be deemed an agent of 
that supplier and subject to all applicable requirements for supplier agents. 

Some Applicants indicated outside entities make sales on their behalf. Anyone 
making sales on behalf of the Applicant, anyone facilitating customers contracting with a 
supplier on behalf of the Applicant, anyone whom the Applicant compensates or to whom 
it provides a commission for facilitating customers contracting with a supplier, and anyone 
with whom the Applicant has an agreement (labeled as an Independent Contractor, 
broker, channel partner, or any other title) to facilitate customers contracting with a 
supplier is an agent of the Applicant for whom the Applicant is responsible. The above 
list is not comprehensive, and all Applicants shall read it with the understanding of the 
Authority’s Motion No. 16 Ruling: there are only three legal entities operating in the 
supplier market in Connecticut (i.e., suppliers, aggregators, and their agents) and no other 
entity may operate in the market. If Applicants have agreements with any entities such 
as those listed above in which the agreement indicates that the entity is not the Applicant’s 
agent, the Applicant must revise or amend such agreements to reflect an agency 
relationship. Further, Applicants must understand their legal responsibilities for anyone 
acting as their agent and interacting with customers, and must train and monitor all agents 
to ensure compliance with Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245o and other applicable law, 
regulations, Authority decisions, orders, and rulings. All Applicants shall annually file in 
their licensing docket a list of all agents working on their behalf (Third-Party Agent form).8 

Certain Applicants requested to serve residential markets. All requests to serve 
residential markets are currently denied. No Applicant provided sufficient information to 
assure the Authority that residential customers would be properly served. As a result, the 
Authority determines that no Applicant has met the burden of demonstrating it is capable 
of serving as an aggregator in the residential market and/or working with residential 
customers. The Authority is permitting the Applicants to serve other customer classes 

a notice containing the following information: (1) The name, address and toll-free customer service 
telephone number of the electric supplier that provides electric generation services under its aggregation 
offer; and (2) The rate for electric generation services stated in its aggregation offer, or a description of 
how electric generation services are charged to customers under its aggregation offer.” 
8 The Third Party Agent form is available on the Authority’s website at: Information for Electric Suppliers at 
the Aggregator Agent Form link. 

5 

based on the information provided because the Authority currently understands that non-
residential customers are more sophisticated market participants with business acumen, 
procurement strategies, and needs, in addition to the procurement of supply.9 Further, 
non-residential customers frequently do not have the freedom to move from supplier to 
supplier at will and without penalty;10 as a result, shopping amongst several rates and 
finding the best one at the time of the contract becomes more imperative for non-
residential customers. 

As part of the application process, EOE reviewed the financial information supplied 
by each Applicant. Although aggregators have less financial exposure than suppliers 
since aggregators do not have renewable portfolio standards and other obligations 
resulting from the supply of energy, aggregators still are liable for their actions and must 
demonstrate sufficient financial capability to serve customers, and further must satisfy 
any penalties if found violating the law. 

Applicants must recognize that in being granted an Electric Aggregator Certificate 
of Registration, they are entering a highly regulated and transparent market. As such, 
they must ensure that their business complies with all applicable laws, including statutes, 
regulations, and Authority decisions, orders, and rulings. The Applicants must accept the 
responsibility of ensuring they maintain knowledge of the legal framework under which 
they function in Connecticut. Equally as important, the Applicants must recognize that 
they solely represent customers in this process and have the responsibility of acting as 
the customer’s agent and working in the customer’s best interest. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-
245o places many obligations and restrictions on aggregators’ engagement with 
customers, and additionally prohibits deceptive marketing and makes any violation 
thereof a violation of the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. Applicants must 
familiarize themselves with the Authority’s application of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245o to 
aggregators and suppliers. Any Applicant found deviating from its legal responsibilities 
and obligations may be subject to prosecution under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-41. 

Each Applicant named herein is granted an Electric Aggregator Certificate of 
Registration to serve all customer classes requested other than residential customers; 
however, all Applicants shall follow all orders contained herein before they are allowed to 
conduct business as an aggregator in Connecticut. 

9 Many Applicants described other services offered to commercial, industrial, and municipal customers, 
such as comprehensive energy management services. 
10 Applicants did not indicate they offered the services necessary to navigate the market in this capacity. 

6 

ORDERS FOR APPLICANTS 

For Orders requiring a filing, each Applicant shall file an electronic version through 
the Authority’s website at www.ct.gov/pura. Submissions filed in compliance with the 
Authority’s Orders must be identified by: Docket Number, Title, and Order Number. 
Compliance with orders shall commence and continue as indicated in each specific Order 
or until an Applicant requests and the Authority approves that an Applicant’s compliance 
is no longer required after a certain date. Unless otherwise provided or determined by 
the Authority, filings submitted in compliance with an order shall constitute satisfaction of 
the Order. Filings requiring Authority approval must be filed as a motion. 

1. Applicants shall serve only commercial, industrial, municipal, or government 
customers, as such categories were requested in each Applicant’s respective 
application. Applicants shall not serve residential customers. 

2. Prior to serving any customer in Connecticut, each Applicant shall revise and/or 
amend all existing contracts with suppliers that contain any form of compensation 
other than the straight pass-through compensation discussed herein. 

3. Prior to serving any customer in Connecticut, each Applicant shall revise and/or 
amend all existing contracts with suppliers that contain any provision implicating 
the aggregator is functioning as the agent of the supplier. 

4. Applicants shall not enter into future contracts with suppliers that do not conform 
to Order Nos. 2 and 3 above. 

5. Prior to serving any customer in Connecticut, each Applicant shall revise and/or 
amend all existing contracts with any entity engaging with customers on the 
Applicant’s behalf and/or being compensated by the Applicant for engaging with 
customers and ensure such contracts reflect an agency between the Applicant and 
that entity. 

6. No later than September 6, 2023, each Applicant shall file copies of contracts 
revised and/or amended pursuant to Order Nos. 2, 3, and/or 5 as a compliance 
filing in its respective licensing docket. 

7. Applicants shall immediately incorporate the use of the Three Customer 
Communications for all future procurements for Connecticut customers and shall 
retain the documentation for three years from the date on which the respective 
document was executed by the customer. 

8. Prior to serving any Connecticut customer, each Applicant shall submit a complete 
Third-Party Agent form in its licensing docket and shall submit such form on or 
before October 15th annually thereafter in its respective licensing docket. If any 
Applicant does not contract with third-party agents, it must still make an annual 
filing indicating so. 

7 

9. Each Applicant shall notify the Authority within 10 days if there are any changes to 
any material filed in its respective application. 

10. Each Applicant shall provide the Authority with any changes to its customer service 
practices, procedures, or policies in writing at least 10 days prior to the effective 
date of such changes. 

11. Each Applicant shall maintain its customer complaint records to indicate: 

a. Date of the complaint; 
b. Name and address of the complainant; 
c. Address or location cited in the complaint; 
d. Description of the complaint; and 
e. Description of the resolution of the complaint. 

12. Pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245(l)(3)(C), each Applicant shall maintain a 
toll-free phone number for customers.

title: PURA Final Decision — Docket 22-09-01: Call Before You Dig, Inc. – Proposed Budget for 2023
text:
STATE OF CONNECTICUT 
PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY 
TEN FRANKLIN SQUARE 
NEW BRITAIN, CT 06051 
DOCKET NO. 22-09-01 CALL BEFORE YOU DIG – PROPOSED BUDGET 
FOR 2023 
December 21, 2022 
By the following Commissioners: 
Marissa P. Gillett 
John W. Betkoski, III 
Michael A. Caron 
DECISION 

Docket No. 22-09-01 

Page 2 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 

A. 
SUMMARY 

The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA or Authority) finds that the 2023 
budget proposed by Call Before You Dig, Inc. (CBYD) is sufficient and reasonable to allow 
CBYD to fulfill its statutorily mandated duties and responsibilities. The Authority also finds 
that the Board has taken steps to maximize the effectiveness of the CBYD program and 
its activities at the lowest possible cost. The Authority will continue to review CBYD 
operations to ensure CBYD functions effectively. The Authority approves the proposed 
budget of $2,544,573, as well as the proposed rates. 

B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 

By application (Application) submitted to the Authority on October 28, 2022, 
pursuant to § 16-345-2(d) of the Regulations of Connecticut State Agencies (Conn. 
Agencies Regs.), CBYD requested Authority approval of its proposed 2023 Operating 
Budget. The Authority reviewed the materials filed and renders this decision. 

C. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 

The Authority recognized the following as Participants to the proceeding: Call 
Before You Dig, Inc., 2040 Whitney Avenue, Hamden, CT 06517; Office of Consumer 
Counsel, Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, CT 06051; and the Commissioner of the 
Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, 79 Elm Street, Hartford, CT, 06106. 

II. 
LEGAL STANDARD 

Section 16-345-2(d) of the Regulations of Connecticut State Agencies requires that 
no less than two months prior to the beginning of each fiscal year, the central 
clearinghouse shall propose to the Authority for approval an annual budget which shall 
include billing rates that shall equitably allocate the costs of operating the notification 
system to those public utilities whose facilities are registered with the central 
clearinghouse. The billing rates are calculated so that the central clearinghouse shall 
neither make a profit nor suffer a loss, but may include reasonable reserves in accordance 
with standard accounting practices to address unforeseen circumstances, provided that 
if such a profit or loss does occur during any year, the budget for the next year shall be 
adjusted accordingly. Id. 

III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 

In the Application, CBYD proposed a 2023 calendar year budget of $2,544,573, 
which represents an increase of 2.4% in operating expenses over the budget from the 
prior year. The proposed budget would increase the monthly mileage rate for member 
utilities by $0.05, to $4.35 per mile per month. Application, p. 1. The monthly mileage 
rate was calculated by dividing the required revenue across the total mileage registered 

Docket No. 22-09-01 

Page 3 

with CBYD. Application, Exhibit A, p. 2. The Authority finds that this will equitably allocate 
the costs of operating the notification system to those public utility companies whose 
facilities are registered with the clearinghouse. 

CBYD projected its 2023 expenses to be $2,570,573, which, with a 2022 budget 
surplus of $26,000, results in a total operating budget of $2,544,573. The projected 2023 
revenue is $2,545,840. Application, Exhibit A, p. 1. The Authority finds that this 
demonstrates that the central clearinghouse shall neither make a profit nor suffer a loss, 
in compliance with Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-345-2(d)(2). 

CBYD is entering into the fourth year of the five-year contract with PelicanCorp 
One-Call, Inc. (PelicanCorp) to manage the day-to-day operations of the call center. 
Application, p. 1. The increase in expense account line item #421 (PelicanCorp contract) 
is a result of the previously approved five-year PelicanCorp contract with CBYD. 
Application, p. 2. The Authority finds that this increase is reasonable and in accordance 
with the PelicanCorp contract. CBYD will begin to negotiate a new contract with 
PelicanCorp during 2023 with a goal of a new contract starting in 2024. Application, p. 1. 
The Authority is supportive of this process as it ensures continuity of operations. 

CBYD is proposing a 200% increase in Expense Account Line item #428 
(Operational System Upgrades). This increase will fund the implementation of a new 
“Coastal Waters” ticket, which will enable CBYD to collaborate with member utilities to 
identify and locate facilities crossing Long Island Sound. Application, p, 2. The Authority 
agrees with this enhancement to the CBYD system. 

The funding of the Operating Capital Reserve line item (Expense Account 940.5) 
is not required in 2023. That account is funded to the auditor’s recommended level of a 
minimum of two months of operating expenses. Application, Exhibit A, p. 7. CBYD shall 
ensure that the contingency fund remains funded at the recommended level. 

The Authority reviewed the annual statement of the financial position of CBYD as 
of December 31, 2021, which was filed by an independent Certified Public Accountant. 
Application, Exhibit B. The Certified Public Accountant is not aware of any material 
modifications required to be made to the financial statements for CBYD to be in conformity 
with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States. Application, Exhibit 
B, p. 2. 

The CBYD Board of Directors (Board) presently meets bi-monthly and various 
committees1 meet on an as-needed basis, but no less frequently than each month in 
which the Board does not meet. This practice should continue. Minutes of all Board 
meetings and committee meetings are to be maintained and provided to the Authority 
within 15 days following the meeting date. Attendance at Board and committee meetings 
is a primary and essential responsibility of all Board members, as is their active 

1 Committees include the Executive Committee, Damage Prevention and Education Committee, Operations 
Committee, and Finance Committee. 

Docket No. 22-09-01 

Page 4 

participation in at least one of the various events conducted during the calendar year. 
The Authority will continue to monitor attendance of Board members. 

IV. 
CONCLUSION 

The Authority finds that the proposed budget is sufficient and reasonable to allow 
CBYD to fulfill its statutorily mandated duties and responsibilities. As such, the Authority 
approves the proposed budget of $2,544,573, along with the proposed rates designed to 
fund such budget.

CALL BEFORE YOU DIG – PROPOSED 
BUDGET FOR 2023

title: PURA Final Decision — Docket 26-01-06: CAPS
text:
STATE OF CONNECTICUT 

PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY 
TEN FRANKLIN SQUARE 
NEW BRITAIN, CT 06051 

DOCKET NO. 26-01-06 
ANNUAL COMMUNITY ACCESS SUPPORT REVIEW 

May 27, 2026 

By the following commissioners: 
Thomas H. Wiehl 
David Arconti, Jr. 
Janice A. Beecher 
Holly H. Cheeseman 
Everett Smith, III 

DECISION 

TABLE OF CONTENTS 
I. 
INTRODUCTION .............................................................................................. 1 
A. SUMMARY..................................................................................................... 1 
B. BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING .............................................................. 1 
C. CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING .................................................................... 1 
D. PARTIES AND INTERVENORS OR PARTICIPANTS .............................................. 1 
II. STANDARD OF REVIEW ................................................................................. 2 
III. AUTHORITY ANALYSIS .................................................................................. 2 
A. CPI CALCULATION ........................................................................................ 2 
B. SOUND VIEW’S WRITTEN COMMENTS ............................................................ 3 
IV. CONCLUSION AND ORDERS ........................................................................ 3 
A. CONCLUSION ................................................................................................ 3 
B. ORDERS ....................................................................................................... 4 
APPENDIX A – 2025 SUBSCRIBER FEE ............................................................. i 
APPENDIX B ........................................................................................................... ii 
APPENDIX C ........................................................................................................... iv 

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
In this Decision, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority) calculates the 
inflation-adjusted amount of community access support required pursuant to General 
Statutes § 16-331a(k). The consumer price index (CPI)1 for the 2025 inflation rate is 
3.25%. The Authority uses this number to determine the 2026 inflation-adjusted amounts 
of community access support required from all multichannel video programming 
distributors (MVPDs). 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
The General Assembly requires the provision of “facilities, equipment, and 
technical and managerial support to enable the production of meaningful community 
access programming within [each] franchise area.” General Statutes § 16-331a(b). 
Through an annual proceeding, the Authority determines “the amount that the company 
or organization responsible for community access operations shall receive for such 
operations from subscribers and from multichannel video programming distributors.” 
General Statutes § 16-331a(k). 

Holders of a Certificate of Cable Franchise Authority (CCFA) or Certificate of Video 
Franchise Authority (CVFA) are required to provide funds in the amount established by 
the Authority. 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On its own motion, the Authority established this docket on December 2, 2025. 
The Authority delegated this matter to its Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement 
(EOE). Notice of Proceeding, p. 1. 
EOE filed a motion to approve a Proposed Final Decision on March 18, 2026. 
Participants had seven days from the filing of EOE’s motion to review the proposed 
decision and to file objections to the motion. 
The Authority issued a proposed final decision (PFD) on April 29, 2026. 
Participants were given the opportunity to provide written comments on the draft decision. 
On May 13, 2026, Sound View Community Media (Sound View) filed written comments. 
D. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS OR PARTICIPANTS 
The Authority designated the Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC), Ten Franklin 
Square, New Britain, Connecticut 06051; EOE, Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, 
Connecticut 06051; The Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, 79 Elm 
Street Hartford, CT 06106-5127; all Connecticut MVPDs; all Connecticut Community 

1 Conn Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-1(2) defines the consumer price index as the United States Department 
of Labor Consumer Price Index, Urban Northeast Region, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. 

Docket No. 26-01-06 

Page 2 

Access Providers (CAPs); and all Connecticut cable advisory councils. A listing of all 
parties, participants, and intervenors is appended hereto as Appendix C.2 
II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
By June 1 of each year, PURA establishes the amount of funding for community 
access operations for each franchise area. See General Statutes § 16-331a(k); Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-10. The amount of funding is determined by adjusting the 
prior year amount by the CPI for the preceding calendar year. Id.3 
The Authority has discretion to conduct a proceeding to increase or decrease the 
statutory subscriber fee by not more than 40%. Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-8(b). 
Specifically, “an entity requesting an increase or decrease [beyond the CPI adjustment] 
shall provide to the [Authority] a clear statement indicating good cause why the request 
should be granted.” Id. If the Authority finds good cause and conducts a proceeding, the 
Authority must hold a hearing and take into consideration the factors articulated in Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-8(d). 
III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
CPI CALCULATION 
The Authority determines herein: (1) the 2025 rate of inflation as measured by the 
CPI for the North n east Urban Regio; (2) the 2026 franchise-specific community access 
support per subscriber amounts; and (3) whether the amounts are within +/-40% of the 
allowed statutory amount, as adjusted for inflation. 
The index values for determining the rate of inflation for 2025 as measured by the 
CPI4 for the Northeast Urban Region are as follows: 
Year 
Dec. 
2024 
327.24 
2025 
337.88 

Based on this data, the 2025 rate of inflation for updating community access 
support amounts pursuant to General Statutes § 16-331a(k) is 3.25%. Since the CPI for 
the Northeast Urban Region increased 3.25% during 2025, the community access 
support amounts are increased by 3.25% as shown in Appendix A. To determine the +/-
40% range within which the Authority may change the per subscriber amount, the 
Authority adjusts the original statutory $5 per subscriber amount for inflation. In its 2025 
Decision the Authority found that the statutory amount as adjusted for inflation was 

2 The Authority requests that all parties, participants, and intervenors inform the Authority of any 
changes/additions to the names, addresses and /or titles in the Appendix C service list. 
3 The General Assembly set the initial amount at five dollars per subscriber per year. 
4 See: https://www.bls.gov/regions/mid-atlantic/data/consumerpriceindexhistorical_northeast_table.htm. 

Docket No. 26-01-06 

Page 3 

$11.49. Increasing this amount by 3.25% for 2025 CPI inflation equates to a value of 
$11.86. Forty percent of $11.86 is $4.74. Consequently, the community access support 
per subscriber must be between $7.12 ($11.86 – $4.74) and $16.60 ($11.86 + $4.74). 
Appendix A demonstrates that the subscriber amounts are properly within this range. 
For the MVPDs “the amount shall be paid on a quarterly basis and shall be 
determined by multiplying the amount per subscriber by the average number of 
subscribers as determined in section 16-331a-9.” Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-7. 
Each MVPD will be ordered to fund community access in 2026 at the inflation-adjusted 
per-subscriber amount shown in Appendix A. 
B. 
SOUND VIEW’S WRITTEN COMMENTS 
Sound View believes the PFD contains inadequacies, including failing to address 
the cord-cutting trend, structural funding reform, and the level of CAP funding. Sound 
View Exceptions, pp. 11-13. Specifically, Sound View argues that the continuously 
declining number of cable television subscribers has resulted in “the structural funding 
crisis confronting community access organizations.” Id., p. 4. Sound View further notes 
that the General Assembly has attempted to address the concerns of community access 
providers through legislation. Id., pp. 5-6. 
Sound View requests, among other things, (1) that the record be supplemented 
with subscriber count data; (2) that the Authority conduct an evaluation of whether the 
current funding mechanism is capable of sustaining community access; and (3) that 
PURA recommend structural reforms to the General Assembly. Id., pp. 13-15. 
The Authority acknowledges that the video content market has and continues to 
evolve significantly and that this evolution directly impacts the funding available for 
community access. The Authority has some discretion under its regulations to adjust the 
annual subscriber fee. However, this discretion does not extend to fundamental changs 
to community access television, including redefining how community access is valued, 
how it is delivered, or who pays for it. These are complex public policy questions involving 
a spectrum of stakeholders (many of whom are not involved in this annual adjustment 
process). The legislative process is the more suitable mechanism for balancing those 
various stakeholder interests. Accordingly, the Authority declines to consider additional 
adjustments to the subscriber fee. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION AND ORDERS 
A. 
CONCLUSION 
The increase in the CPI for the Northeast Urban Region during calendar year 2025 
is 3.25%. The franchise-specific inflation adjustments calculated in this Decision apply to 
all Connecticut MVPDs and community access providers. The 2026 Subscriber Fee 
required of each MVPD is set forth in Appendix A. 

Docket No. 26-01-06 

Page 4 

B. 
ORDERS 
For the following Orders, the Company shall file an electronic version through the 
Authority’s website at www.ct.gov/pura. Submissions filed in compliance with the 
Authority’s Orders must be identified by all three of the following: Docket Number, Title 
and Order Number. Compliance with orders shall commence and continue as indicated 
in each specific Order or until the Company requests and the Authority approves that the 
Company’s compliance is no longer required after a certain date. 

1. 
Effective July 1, 2026, and continuing for twelve (12) months, each MVPD shall 
fund community access using the 2026 Subscriber Fee shown in Appendix A for 
each franchise service area in which it provides video service. Frontier shall fund 
community access using the 2026 Subscriber Fee shown in Appendix A for each 
franchise service area in which it provides video service, and shall file, as a 
compliance filing, the Subscriber Fee and total amount paid for each franchise 
service area in which it provides service. 

2. 
All Advisory Councils shall file their 2026 Annual Report no later than January 31, 
2027, under the current Docket Number. 

3. 
All Community Access Providers shall file their 2026 Community Access Report 
no later than February 15, 2027, under the current Docket Number. 

4. 
The designated community access providers, advisory councils, parties, 
intervenors and MVPDs shall inform the Authority of any changes/additions to the 
names, addresses and /or titles in the Appendix C service list.

ANNUAL COMMUNITY ACCESS SUPPORT REVIEW

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) approves the 
acquisition by Charter Communications, Inc. (Charter, Applicant, or Company) of certain 
subsidiaries of Cox Communications, Inc. The Authority finds that Charter possesses the 
requisite financial, technological, and managerial suitability, that the Company has 
demonstrated the ability to provide safe, adequate, and reliable service to the public, and 
that the proposed transaction is in the public interest, subject to compliance with the 
orders contained herein. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
On May 16, 2025, Cox Enterprises Inc. (CEI), Charter, and Charter 
Communications Holdings, LLC (Charter Holdings) entered into an agreement in which 
Charter will acquire Cox Communications, Inc. (Cox) and its subsidiaries, and in 
exchange CEI will receive cash and equity in Charter Holdings. Application, Aug. 5, 2025, 
Docket No. 25-08-11, Application of Charter Communications, Inc. for Approval of a 
Change of Control, p. 1 (Application). On August 5, 2025, pursuant to General Statutes 
§ 16-47 and Conn. Agencies Regs. §§ 16-47-1 et seq., Charter submitted the Application 
to the Authority requesting approval to acquire three Cox subsidiaries (Proposed 
Transaction), specifically Cox Connecticut Telcom, LLC; Cox Strategic Services, LLC; 
and CoxCom, LLC (collectively, Cox Licensees.) Id. 
C. 
PARTIES IN INTEREST 
Charter is a publicly traded Delaware corporation headquartered at 400 
Washington Boulevard in Stamford, Connecticut 06902. Application, p. 3. Charter and 
its operating subsidiaries provide broadband and cable services to 31.2 million customers 
in 41 states, including Connecticut. Id. Charter’s Connecticut subsidiaries include: (1) 
Charter Fiberlink CT-CCO, LLC which provides competitive local exchange and 
interexchange telecommunications services; (2) Spectrum Northeast, LLC which 
provides cable services; (3) Spectrum Advance Services, LLC and Charter Enabled IP 
Services, LLC provide Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) services; and (4) Spectrum
