II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
Under General Statutes § 16-47, no person may take any action that directly or 
indirectly causes a change of control over certain regulated companies, including 
regulated telecommunications companies and their holding companies, “without first 
making written application to and obtaining the approval of the Public Utilities Regulatory 
Authority” in a contested proceeding. 
“Holding company” is defined as “any corporation, association, partnership, trust 
or similar organization, or person” with control over a regulated company. General 
Statutes § 16-47(a)(1). 
The Authority interprets General Statutes § 16-47(a)(2) as defining control as a 
factual determination that may be found by the Authority under one of two alternative 
bases, which for convenience the Authority refers to as (1) presumptive control and (2) 
directive control. 
Presumptive control applies when “a person directly or indirectly owns” a threshold 
percentage of the voting securities of a regulated company or holding company.5 General 
Statutes § 16-47(a)(2). Once possession of the threshold percentage is established, a 
presumption of control arises unless “rebutted by a showing that such ownership does 
not in fact confer control.” Id. As the Cox Licensees are telecommunications companies 
and a holding company thereof, the threshold percentage applicable to this proceeding is 
40% of the voting securities. Id. 

5 The threshold percentage is set by statute at 10% of the voting securities of a gas company, electric 
distribution company, water company, telephone company, community antenna television company; or 
40% of the voting securities of a holder of a certificate of cable franchise authority, certified 
telecommunications provider, or certified competitive video service provider, or its holding company. 
General Statutes § 16-47(a)(2). 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 7 

Directive control applies when a person possesses “the power to direct or cause 
the direction of the management and policies of a [regulated company] or a holding 
company, whether through ownership of its voting securities, the ability to effect a change 
in the composition of its board of directors or otherwise.” Id. The Authority interprets 
directive control as a factual determination that must be supported by evidence on the 
record demonstrating the ability to direct the company, but one that is not constrained to 
any specific definition of “the power to direct.”6 
Upon receipt of an application for approval of change of control over a regulated 
company, the Authority “shall investigate and hold a public hearing . . . and thereafter may 
approve or disapprove any such application in whole or in part and upon such terms and 
conditions as it deems necessary or appropriate.” General Statutes § 16-47(d)(2). 
Specifically, the Authority shall evaluate the following: 
(1) 
the financial, technological, and managerial suitability and responsibility of the 
applicant; and 

(2) 
the legal, financial and technical ability of the subject of the application to provide 
safe, adequate, and reliable service to the public through the company's plant, 
equipment, and manner of operation if the application were to be approved. 

Id. 
The purpose of General Statutes § 16-47 is “to assure to the state of Connecticut 
its full powers to regulate its public service companies, to increase the powers of the 
Public Utilities Regulatory Authority and to promote local control of the public service 
companies of this state.” General Statutes § 16-11. Accordingly, where statutory 
interpretation is required, the Authority construes such statutes in a manner that furthers 
this legislative purpose. 
As the Proposed Transaction involves “the transfer of ownership of assets or a 
franchise of a public service company,” General Statutes § 16-22 tasks the Applicant with 
“the burden of proving . . . that said transfer of assets or franchise is in the public interest.” 
Furthermore, because the Proposed Transaction concerns the provision of 
telecommunications services in the State of Connecticut, the Authority is statutorily 
required to regulate in a manner that fosters competition and protects the public interest. 
General Statutes § 16-247f(a).

that the definition of direction not be limited in scope to the statutorily enumerated examples—in other 
words, these examples “do not constitute an exhaustive or exclusive list.” Casey v. Lamont, 338 Conn. 
479, 492 (2021) (finding a list similarly inexhaustive where it used the phrase “including, but not limited 
to”); see also Sams v. DEEP, 308 Conn. 359, 385 (2013) (“or by any other suitable means”); State v. 
Jones, 51 Conn. App. 126, 137 (Conn. App. Ct. 1998) (“such as”).

Because the term “public interest” is not defined in Title 16, the Authority’s 
construction of the term is governed by General Statutes § 1-1(a).7 Public interest is 
commonly defined as “a specific public benefit or stake in something.”8 The Applicant 
must demonstrate that the Proposed Transaction provides a public benefit or advances 
the public’s stake. The purpose of public interest review under General Statutes §§ 16-
22 and 16-247f(a) is therefore to ensure that the benefits of a transaction involving a 
public service company accrue not just to shareholders but to all stakeholders. 
Consequently, public interest review is distinct from the suitability analysis conducted 
under General Statutes § 16-47(d). See Aquarion Water Authority v. Public Utilities 
Regulatory Authority, Superior Court, judicial district of New Britain, Docket No. CV-25-
6101571-S, p. 9 n. 2 (January 15, 2026) (rejecting the argument that section 16-22’s 
public interest analysis is “coextensive” with the factors in section 16-47(d)).

its service offerings to incorporate technological advances, including launching a 
streaming box product that provides instant access to Spectrum TV and other streaming 
apps; multiple tiers of its Contour video packages to meet varying customer needs; and 
increased product compatibility and integration with smart TVs. See Interrog. Resp. 
PURA-3. 
Post-transaction, Charter plans to extend its content provider agreements to the 
Cox footprint. Interrog. Resp. PURA-1. This will benefit current Cox customers by 
allowing access to the content provided under these agreements without having to pay 
for supplemental subscriptions. Id. Existing Cox customers may choose between 
switching to a Charter plan or retaining their existing Cox plan. Hr’g. Tr., Nov. 19, 2025, 
87:15–88:1. 
The Authority reviewed Charter’s leadership team, the potential benefits of the 
combined resources with Cox, and the Company’s responsiveness to adapt to market 
changes and offer products and services that consumers want. The Authority determines 
that the proposed transaction meets the managerial suitability and responsibility 
requirements. However, during the proceeding Charter and Cox conveyed that it was 
premature to provide detailed information regarding operational integration planning and 
managerial and/or leadership changes post-transaction. Interrog. Resp. OCC-34 and 
Hr’g. Tr., Nov. 19, 2025, 98:12–25. 
The Authority is concerned about post-transaction integration decisions that could 
adversely impact the Connecticut workforce, customer service, or positions migrating 
from the Stamford headquarters to Cox’s headquarters in Atalanta, Georgia. In their joint 
brief, the OCC and AG, suggested various measures to ensure that Connecticut interests 
are protected, should the Authority approve the transaction. OCC/OAG Brief, Dec. 22, 
2025, pp. 33–35 (OCC/OAG Brief). Under the terms of the proposed settlement 
agreement, the Company agreed to multiple measures and requirements negotiated with 
the OCC and OAG to ensure that Connecticut customers and that state’s interests are 
protected. Notably, the Company will provide a detailed integration plan within 90 days 
after the transaction. Settlement Agreement, No. 23, p. 4. Based on the record in this 
proceeding, Charter meets the managerial capability and suitability requirements to 
manage the Cox Licensees. 
2. Telecom Certification & Video Franchise Authority 
Charter and Cox have provided services in Connecticut for decades, and both 
companies have sought and received regulatory approval from the Authority on several 
occasions. In 2004, the Authority granted Charter’s subsidiary, Charter Fiberlink CT-
CCO, LLC a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) to provide 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 13 

competitive 
local 
exchange 
and 
interexchange 
telecommunications 
services. 
Application, p. 4. In 2007, the Authority granted Charter Communications of Western 
Connecticut a Certificate of Cable Franchise Authority (CCFA) to provide video services 
and to own, lease, maintain, operate, manage or control facilities in, under or over any 
public highway in the delivery of such service, subject to the laws of the state. Id., p. 5. 
In 2008, the Authority granted Charter Communications Entertainment I, LLC d/b/a 
Charter Communications of Northeastern Connecticut a CCFA to provide video services 
and to own, lease, maintain, operate, manage, or control facilities in, under or over any 
public highway in the delivery of such service, subject to the laws of the state. Id. 
Similarly, Cox has obtained Authority approval for telecommunications and video 
services. In June 1997, the Authority granted Cox Connecticut Telecom, LLC a CPCN to 
operate as a reseller and facilities-based provider of intrastate telecommunications 
services in Connecticut, including competitive local exchange service. Application, p. 7. 
In November 2007, the Authority granted CoxCom Inc., CCFAs in its Enfield, Manchester 
and Meriden franchise areas to provide video services and to own, lease, maintain, 
operate, manage or control facilities in, under or over any public highway in the delivery 
of such service, subject to the laws of the state. Id. In 2012, the Authority authorized 
CoxCom to provide statewide video service outside of its franchise area. Id. 
In each CPCN approval, the Authority found that the company possessed and 
demonstrated adequate financial resources, managerial ability and technical competency 
to provide the proposed service as required by General Statutes § 16-247g (b). The 
CCFA and CVA approvals relied on affidavits that affirmed that the application met all the 
requirements of Connecticut Public Act, No, 07-253, An Act Concerning Certified 
Competitive Video Service (the Act). These requirements include Company affirmations 
regarding (1) principal place of business (2) timely filings with the Federal 
Communications Commission (FCC) in advance of offering such video service in 
Connecticut, (3) compliance with all applicable federal and state statutes and regulations 
and Authority orders, and compliance with the Act. 
Based on the foregoing, the Authority finds that Charter and Cox have an 
established presence in Connecticut and have previously demonstrated the technical, 
financial and managerial suitability required for certification. Although certification 
requirements significantly overlap with the requirements of General Statutes § 16-47, 
dramatic changes in technology and the video and communications markets in the years 
since certification, paired with the differing scope of review between certification and 
change of control proceedings, mean these findings are not directly comparable. 
Therefore, the Authority focuses its review on Charter’s response to changes in the video 
content market, in addition to evidence on the experience and qualification of its 
leadership team and its ability to deliver quality service and sufficiently build and maintain 
its Connecticut network. 
E. 
PROVISION OF SAFE, ADEQUATE, AND RELIABLE SERVICE 
In accordance with General Statutes § 16-47(d)(2), the Authority reviewed the 
ability of Charter to provide safe, adequate, and reliable service to the public. The record 
indicates that Charter has access to a large pool of personnel, critical equipment and 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 14 

redundant networks within their service territory, which will facilitate its ability to deliver 
safe, adequate, and reliable service for customers of the Cox Licensees. Application, p. 
28. Recently Charter was also recognized by the publication Newsweek as being one of 
the most trustworthy companies in America and was the only cable operator to receive 
this distinction. Application, p. 24. Charter also has four customer commitment pillars it 
will implement across its new territories (1) reliable connectivity, (2) transparency at every 
step, (3) exceptional services, and (4) always improving. Charter Brief, p. 20. 
Additionally, same-day scheduling has increased dramatically while next-day and two-
day scheduling has declined precipitously, demonstrating that Charter has been 
responding to customers in an expeditious manner. Interrog. Resp. PURA-17. 
Additionally, under General Statutes § 16-32e(b), the Authority reviews the 
Emergency Response Plans (ERPs) of telecommunications companies10 and submits a 
biennial report to the Energy and Technology Committee of the Connecticut General 
Assembly. Both Charter and Cox have submitted filings for this process in previous years. 
See, e.g., Report, Aug. 30, 2024, Docket No. 24-02-03, 2024 PURA Review of and Report 
on Connecticut Public Service Company Emergency Response Plans (ERP Report). In 
the ERP Report, the Authority stated that the submitted ERPs were compliant with the 
three requirements of General Statutes § 16-32e(b), which requires telecommunications 
companies to provide (1) key points of contact for emergencies, (2) information on 
participation in statewide exercises, and (3) response procedures affecting incremental 
percentages of customer outages. ERP Report, p. 10. 
Charter claims one of the major advantages of the Proposed Transaction will be 
gaining access to Cox’s Enterprise-grade cloud backup and disaster recovery solutions. 
Charter Brief, pp. 23–24. The Transaction will thus enable the combined company to offer 
a more comprehensive suite of disaster preparedness and business continuity solutions 
to Connecticut’s public safety agencies, municipalities, and essential service providers. 
Id. 
The Authority recognizes the importance of robust cybersecurity and data privacy 
policies to protect both Charter and its customers. ERP Report, pp. 10–12. At the 
evidentiary hearing, CEI reported that it had experienced a cybersecurity incident that 
had affected several Connecticut residents. Evidentiary Hr’g., Tr. Nov. 21, 2025, pp. 34–
35. Both OCC and OAG express concern over Charter’s cybersecurity and compliance 
with Section 42-522 of the Connecticut Data Privacy Act, and suggest that Charter and 
Cox file an integration plan that includes security practices and policies. OCC/OAG Brief, 
pp. 18–19. Historically, the Authority has allowed similar commitments as part of the 
settlements between telecommunications companies. See, e.g., Decision, June 11, 
2025, Docket No. 24-11-06, Joint Application of Verizon Communications Inc. and Frontier 
Communications Parent, Inc. for Approval of a Change of Control, pp. 1–2, 14. 

10 Within the ERP report, the Authority uses the term “telecommunications companies” as a collective term 
that refers to Incumbent Local Exchange Carriers (ILECs), companies holding a Certificate of Cable 
Franchise Authority (CCFA) or a Certificate of Video Franchise Authority (CVFA), and facilities-based 
telecommunications providers. ERP Report, p. 10. 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 15 

Based on the foregoing, the Authority finds that Charter has the capability to 
provide safe, adequate, and reliable service to customers upon the closing of the 
Proposed Transaction. 
F. 
PUBLIC INTEREST 
In accordance with General Statutes §§ 16-22 and 16-247f(a), the Authority 
reviewed the impact of the Proposed Transaction on competition and the public interest. 
The record indicates that the Proposed Transaction will have minimal impact on 
competition and is consistent with the public interest. 
1. Competitive Effects 
Charter and Cox operate in largely non-overlapping service territories in 
Connecticut, with only 46 overlapping broadband-serviceable locations out of 
approximately 1.5 million. Interrog. Resp. PURA-12, p. 7. As OCC and OAG observed, 
this represents a 0.003% overlap rate. OAG/OCC Brief, p. 25. Consequently, the 
Authority finds that the Proposed Transaction has virtually no impact on direct 
competition. 
Charter contends that the Transaction will "enhance competition" by introducing 
bundled products. Application, p. 15. Charter and Cox assert the Transaction will bring 
"numerous benefits—without any countervailing harms." Charter/Cox Reply Brief, Jan. 
8, 2026, p. 1. Charter asserts that the combined company will bring "financial strength, 
product depth, capital resources, and unparalleled technology, tools and training" to 
Connecticut. Application, p. 15. However, when asked to quantify these benefits for 
Connecticut specifically, Charter acknowledged that synergies "have not been calculated 
on a state-by-state basis." Interrog. Resp. PURA-9. 
The elimination of Cox as one of Charter’s direct competitors is likely to reduce 
future competition within their respective service territories. See, e.g., Interrog. Resp. 
PURA-12, p. 1 (stating that “Charter and Cox are not statutory monopolies”). The record 
also indicates potential impact on indirect or substitute competition, with Charter 
acknowledging that it faces "robust competition" from various alternative service 
providers. Id. However, because this decision is limited to the Cox Licensees, the 
Authority finds the competitive impact of the Proposed Transaction does not require 
remedial action. 
2. Workforce Impact 
The Authority considers job loss or other harmful impact on the Connecticut 
workforce to be of substantial public interest within the meaning of General Statutes §§ 
16-22 and 16-247f(a), and has reviewed the record for evidence of downsizing or 
workforce reduction caused by the Proposed Transaction. 
On October 21, 2025, Charter laid off approximately 1,200 administrative 
employees, including employees in Connecticut. See Hr’g Tr., Nov. 21, 2025, 284:15–
285:7. Record evidence also reflects large reductions in force from call center closures. 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 16 

See Tr., 288:2–289:15. Although Charter did not provide concrete numbers for 
anticipated layoffs, testimony acknowledged the merger would produce “some duplication 
of roles” that could have “workforce implications” in Connecticut and nationally. See Hr’g 
Tr., Nov. 19, 2025, 103:9–10 and 19–20; 104:21–105:1. When specifically asked about 
redundancies at Charter’s Stamford headquarters, Charter acknowledged “there will be 
some duplication in functions” due to the merger. See Tr., 106:6–19. 
The Authority remains concerned about the impact of the Proposed Transaction 
on the Connecticut workforce. Nonetheless, due to Charter’s commitment to maintaining 
its Stamford headquarters pursuant to the Settlement Agreement and the consumer 
benefits previously discussed in this decision, the Authority finds that the Proposed 
Transaction is consistent with the public interest. 
3. Settlement Agreement 
Charter, CEI, Cox, OAG, and OCC (collectively, Settling Parties) requested that 
the Authority approve the Settlement Agreement submitted by the Settling Parties. Motion 
No. 34, p. 1. According to the Settling Parties, the Settlement Agreement “resolves issues 
related to the Application . . . raised by OCC and the OAG and provides numerous 
commitments, including consumer billing and fee protections and transparency, service 
reliability and outage-related assurances and reporting, customer service and consumer 
protections, video-service related pledges, regulatory cooperation, Connecticut presence 
commitments, privacy and post-closing integration reporting, digital inclusion investment 
commitments, and other commitments.” Id., p. 1. 
Specifically, the Settlement Agreement contains 38 enumerated terms. Motion No. 
34, Ex. 1. Term Nos. 1 through 25 and Term No. 29 constitute various post-transaction 
commitments by Charter (Charter Commitments). See id., pp. 1–5. Term No. 26 contains 
a commitment that OCC and OAG will “not continue to litigate” their position on the 
pledging of assets or CEI’s post-transaction acquisition of equity in Charter. Id., p. 5. The 
remaining items concern the Settlement Agreement itself, including non-severability, 
choice of law, limitations on amendment, and terms governing execution of the Settlement 
Agreement. See id., pp. 5–6. No parties opposed the Settlement Agreement. 
The Charter Commitments are intended to address of range of issues, including 
(1) affordability and billing, (2) network management and operations, (3) consumer 
protection and customer service, (4) video services, (5) regulatory cooperation and 
reporting, and (6) Connecticut presence and investment. Motion No. 34, pp. 3–5. 
The Authority “may, whenever it deems appropriate and is consistent with the 
principles set forth in sections 16-19 and 16-19e, adopt proposed settlements produced 
by alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to resolve contested cases and 
proceedings.” General Statutes § 16-19jj(a). Here, the Authority appreciates the 
collective effort of the Settling Parties to address and resolve a significant number of 
disputed issues in this proceeding. Importantly, the Settlement Agreement and, more 
particularly, the Charter Commitments included therein, support and are an important 
factor in finding that that the Proposed Transaction is in the public interest. 

Docket No. 25-08-11 
Page 17 

Accordingly, in determining that the Proposed Transaction satisfies the public 
interest standard under General Statutes §§ 16-22 and 16-247f(a), the Authority adopts 
and incorporates the Settlement Agreement into this decision.11 The Settlement 
Agreement is attached as Exhibit 1. The Authority’s approval of the Proposed 
Transaction is, therefore, conditioned upon and subject to compliance with the 
enumerated orders below. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION AND ORDERS 
A. 
CONCLUSION 
The Authority finds that Charter possesses the requisite technological, managerial, 
and financial suitability to operate a public service company and to provide safe, 
adequate, and reliable service to the public. Additionally, the Authority finds that the 
Proposed Transaction is in the public interest. Consequently, the Authority approves the 
Proposed Transaction subject to compliance with the Orders set forth in Section Error! 
Reference source not found.., Error! Reference source not found., which incorporate 
terms of the Settlement Agreement. 
B. 
ORDERS

or until the Company requests and the Authority approves that the Company’s compliance

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) allocates 
$1,988,010.51 in grants from the Public, Educational and Governmental Programming 
and Education Technology Investment Account (PEGPETIA). The Authority awards 
PEGPETIA funds accumulated through February 28, 2025, in this proceeding, with 
$995,132.19 for 33 grants to support public, educational, and governmental programming 
(PEG Grants) and $992,878.32 for 81 grants to support educational technology initiatives 
(ETI Grants). 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
In 2007, the General Assembly established the PEGPETIA program to promote 
and improve public, educational, and governmental programming and to support 
education technology initiatives. See Public Act No. 07-253, § 33, codified as General 
Statutes § 16-331cc. The program is funded by a quarterly tax on the gross earnings of 
video service providers. General Statutes § 16-331cc. 
Since 2022, the Authority has conducted annual proceedings to determine the 
allocation of accumulated funding in the account and to administer grants to eligible 
entities. The Authority established the application requirements through a contested 
proceeding in 2008 and revised the requirements in 2019. Decision, Mar. 26, 2008, 
Docket No. 07-10-11, DPUC Proceeding to Establish Administrative Guidelines for the 
Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Educational Technology 
Investment Account Pursuant to Public Act 07-253 (Guidelines Decision); Decision, Oct. 
23, 2019, Docket No. 07-10-11RE01, DPUC Proceeding to Establish Administrative 
Guidelines for the Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Education 
Technology Investment Account – Grant Eligibility Criteria and Guidelines (Revised 
Guidelines Decision); General Statutes § 16-331cc(d); Corresp., Nov. 20, 2019, Docket 
No. 19-11-01, Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Education 
Technology Investment Account Program Pursuant to Public Act 07-253 (PEGPETIA 
Educational Grant Guidance). 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On September 1, 2024, the Authority issued a Notice of Proceeding, which notified 
prospective applicants that all grant applications must be submitted by February 28, 2025. 
The Authority received a total of 136 applications, filed as motions, during the 
application window, September 1, 2024, through February 28, 2025. 
The Authority issued a proposed final decision in this matter on March 21, 2025. 
All participants were given the opportunity to file written exceptions to the proposed final 
decision. One participant also filed an objection to another participant’s application. 
D. 
PARTICIPANTS 
A list of participants is attached as Appendix A. 

Docket No. 24-10-02 
Page 2

II. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
INTRODUCTION 
In this proceeding, the Authority awards $1,988,010.51 of PEGPETIA funds 
accumulated through February 28, 2025.1 The Authority awards 50% of PEGPETIA grant 
funding to: (1) local community antenna television and video advisory councils; (2) the 
state-wide video advisory council; (3) public, educational, and governmental 
programmers; and (4) public, educational, and governmental studio operators, “to 
subsidize capital and equipment costs related to producing and procuring [public,

Authority awards the remaining 50% of PEGPETIA grant funding “to boards of education 
and other education entities for education technology initiatives.” Id. 
B. 
USE OF PEGPETIA GRANT FUNDS 
1. PEG Grant Permissible Uses 
PEG Grant funds must be used for capital and equipment costs that aid the 
production or procurement of public, educational, and governmental programs for use on 
a cable television channel. PEG Grant funding is intended to promote and improve public, 
educational, and governmental access programming in Connecticut. Guidelines 
Decision, p. 2. Although funds are available to a wide variety of entities involved either 
directly or indirectly in producing community access programs, the awarding of funds to 
those entities is not the goal of the program. Id. The goal of PEG Grant funding is to 
“increase the quantity, quality and variety of community access productions made 
available to Competitive Video Service Providers (CVSP) and Community Antenna 
Television (CATV2) subscribers.” Guidelines Decision, p. 2. 
In each franchise area in Connecticut, a company or organization may be selected 
to assume responsibility for community access operations. General Statutes § 16-
331a(b)–(c). “Each franchise holder3 shall maintain at least one specially designated 
channel to be used for community access.” Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-2(a). The 
Authority has defined the term Community Access Provider (CAP) as “the entity 
responsible for providing community access operations within a franchise area.” Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-1(1). Each CAP is required to provide “facilities, equipment, 
and technical and managerial support to enable the production of meaningful community 
access programming within [each] franchise area. Each company shall include all its 
community access channels in its basic service package.” General Statutes § 16-
331a(b). “Community access” means public access, educational access and

community access channel for non-commercial educational programming.”4 Conn.

Accordingly, PEG Grant funds must be used for capital and equipment costs that 
aid the production or procurement of public, educational, and governmental programs for 
broadcast on Connecticut community access channels.5 After receiving a PEG Grant, 
recipients must file a report with the Authority, stating: (a) the title, subject, and duration

PEGPETIA funds are made available to the applicant’s local PEG studio.6 
Awarded PEG Grant funds may be applied toward expenses related to any capital 
and investment project listed in the application that aid the production or procurement of 
public, educational, and governmental programs for broadcast on Connecticut community 
access channels, with less than 10% used for non-equipment costs.7

persistent misunderstanding of the concept of the “separation of church and state” 
doctrine, the Authority reminds participants that the allocation of funding is made for 
capital and equipment costs that aid the production or procurement of public, educational, 
and governmental programs for broadcast on Connecticut community access channels.

2. ETI Grant Permissible Uses 
ETI Grant funding is intended to support education technology initiatives of boards 
of education and other education entities. General Statutes § 16-331cc(b) provides that 
half of PEGPETIA funds “shall be available to boards of education and other education 
entities for education technology initiatives.” Accordingly, ETI Grant funds should be used 
to support education technology initiatives of boards of education and other education 
entities. 
The term “education technology initiatives” is not defined in by General Statutes § 
16-331cc. In the Guidelines Decision, the Authority’s predecessor stated: 
The Department also believes that by including the phrase “education 
technology investment fund” in the definition of the account, the 
Legislature’s goal is to increase the quantity, quality and variety of 
educational programming currently being produced in Connecticut by 
public, educational and government studios, boards of education and other 
educational entities. 
Guidelines Decision, pp. 2–3. 
Subsequently, however, the Authority considered “term ‘education technology 
initiatives’ as it is used in [General Statutes] § 16-331cc(b) regarding the allocation of 
grant funds” in response to inquiries. PEGPETIA Educational Grant Guidance, p. 1. The 
Authority noted that it had not previously addressed the issue and offered the following 
guidance: 
The term “education technology initiatives” is not defined in the PEGPETIA 
statute, but the General Assembly has expressed its understanding of 
education technology through Chapter 61a of Title 4d of the General 
Statutes, which is entitled “Education Technology” and establishes a 
committee to implement state-wide education technology goals. In 
particular, under [General Statutes] § 4d-80(c)(2), the General Assembly 
articulated the following education technology goals: 
(A) Connecting all institutions of higher education, libraries, public 
elementary and secondary schools, regional educational service centers 
and other parties through a state-wide high speed, flexible network that will 
allow for video, voice and data transmission; 
(B) Wiring all school classrooms and connecting them to the Internet and to 
the state-wide high speed network through wired, wireless, or any other 
digital transmission technology providing high speed connectivity; 
(C) Providing access for all public schools, public libraries and libraries at 
institutions of higher education to a core set of on-line full text resources

maximize buying power; 
(D) Ensuring, in cooperation with the State Board of Education, competency

In addition, the Commission for Education Technology (CET) has issued a 
number of reports and guidance documents. On June 26, 2017, the CET

In light of these expressly stated goals and core focus areas related to 
education technology, the Authority will interpret the term “education 
technology initiatives” as applying to projects that advance or are consistent 
with at least one of these goals or focus area 
PEGPETIA Educational Grant Guidance, pp. 1–2. 
Awarded ETI Grant funds may be applied toward the expenses related to any

appropriately, ETI Grant recipients must file a report of the project enabled by the grant

2. PEG Grant Allocation 
For this grant cycle, the Authority has capped funding for PEG studios at $49,000 
and for PEG programmers at $10,000. In the Revised Guidelines Decision, the Authority 
noted the problems inherent in providing PEG Grant funding to individuals. See Revised 
Guidelines Decision, p. 2 (recognizing “the value that individuals may bring to community 
access programming but agree[ing] with commenters that awarding grants to individuals 
is not an efficient use of PEGPETIA funds.”). The Authority also noted that 
Equipment purchased by individuals is not broadly available to the public or 
programming community and, therefore, has a much more limited impact. 
In addition, individual grants impose administrative burdens with respect to 
auditing and compliance. Importantly, PEG studios are required to maintain 
video production equipment and to make the equipment available to 
programmers. 
The Authority believes that the goals of the Act are best achieved by 
increasing the availability, quantity, and quality of equipment at local studios 
so that the greatest number of individuals have the ability to produce 
programming utilizing state of the art equipment and facilities. 
Revised Guidelines Decision, pp. 2–3 (citing General Statutes § 16-331a(b) and Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-11). 
The Authority’s concerns, as expressed in the Revised Guidelines Decision, are 
similarly applicable to providing PEG funding to individual PEG programmer organizations 
whose central mission is not producing television content. Many non-studio organizations 
received large amounts of funding in the past few grant cycles and provided compliance 
showing little to no programming provided to local access channels. Meanwhile, grants 
provided to PEG studios resulted in significantly more programming for local access 
channels. The Authority recognizes that some non-studio grant recipients provided more 
content to local access channels, however, those appear to be exceptions to the typical 
results.

for PEG programmers at $10,000 is appropriate. Table 5, below, provides the specific

G. 
FUTURE GRANT CYCLES 
In the future, the Authority intends to administer PEGPETIA grant funds in a 
biennial docket. The lengthened grant cycles will provide several benefits, including (1) 
providing grant recipients with additional time to complete projects and demonstrate 
compliance with Authority orders, (2) allowing the Authority to better allocate funding to 
PEG Grant applicants with a demonstrated record of producing PEG programming for the 
community access channels, (3) allowing the Authority to place higher caps on grant 
awards, and (4) reducing the administrative burden on applicants associated with annual 
applications and compliance. 
A biennial docket allows for a longer grant cycle, in which recipients have nearly a 
year to use grant funding and comply with the Authority’s orders. In turn, the Authority 
and docket participants can review compliance filings to ensure completeness and 
determine eligibility for future grant awards before a new docket is opened. That timing 
will allow for greater accountability, particularly with respect to how much PEG 
programming is produced and provided to community access channels using PEG Grant 
funds. The Authority anticipates that PEG Grant recipients will make capital investments 
in the months following disbursement of funds, allowing for sufficient time to produce and 
submit programming to the community access channels before the compliance deadline. 
Accordingly, the Authority will have sufficient information to allocate funding to promote 
and improve public, educational, and governmental programming.

The Authority anticipates that recent reductions in the funding available in recent 
dockets will continue as cable subscriptions continue to decline. Allocating grant funds 
every other year will allow sufficient PEGPETIA funds to accumulate for recipients to 
undertake meaningful investments using grant funds. In addition, the amount of available 
funding would be known at the start of each proceeding, allowing applicants to more 
accurately plan to use allocated funding. 
Finally, the total amount of available funding would remain unaffected by the length 
of the grant cycle, which would allow grant recipients to receive the same funding but 
apply (and comply) half as often. The application window could also be shortened, 
permitting the Authority and docket participants more time in which to review applications 
for eligibility (and potentially allow grant applicants a larger window of time in which to 
correct deficiencies in their applications).

title: PURA Final Decision — Docket 24-01-41: Transfer Comm. Access
text:
STATE OF CONNECTICUT 

PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY 
TEN FRANKLIN SQUARE 
NEW BRITAIN, CT 06051 

DOCKET NO. 24-01-41 
REQUEST TO TRANSFER COMMUNITY 
ACCESS PROVIDER DESIGNATION 

August 7, 2024 

Marissa P. Gillett 
John W. Betkoski, III 
Michael A. Caron 

DECISION 

TABLE OF CONTENTS 
I. 
INTRODUCTION .......................................................................................... 1 
A. SUMMARY ................................................................................................ 1 
B. CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING ................................................................ 1 
C. PARTIES AND INTERVENORS ..................................................................... 1 
II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW ............................................................................ 1 
III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS .............................................................................. 2 
A. BRASS CITY APPLICATION ........................................................................ 2 
IV. 
CONCLUSION AND ORDERS .................................................................... 5 
A. CONCLUSION ........................................................................................... 5 
B. ORDERS ................................................................................................... 5 

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) directs Brass City 
Community Television, Inc. (Brass City) to assume the Community Access Provider 
designation as well as the responsibilities for and the control of operations at the access 
facility, which are currently designated to and controlled by Skye Cable XII, Inc. (Skye). 
B. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On January 11, 2024, Skye filed an inquiry with the Authority as to the procedure 
to transfer its Community Access Provider designation as well as responsibility for and 
control of operations of the access facility (Inquiry). On March 4, 2024, the Authority 
issued a Notice of Proceeding and Procedural Order (NOP) directing Skye to file an 
accounting of its assets addressing the process for nonprofits to request to assume 
responsibility. The Authority requested that any community-based nonprofit organization 
that desired to assume responsibility for the Company’s community access operations 
file a petition with the Authority in accordance with General Statutes § 16-331a(c) not later 
than April 8, 2024. NOP. 
On March 19, 2024, Skye filed an accounting of its assets. Skye Corresp., Mar. 19, 
2024. The Authority received a petition to assume responsibility for Skye’s community 
access provider operations from Brass City on April 8, 2024. Brass City Corresp., Apr. 4, 
2024 (Petition). 
The Authority offered parties and intervenors the opportunity for a hearing with a 
date certain to request the hearing. Notice of Hearing, May 29, 2024. No parties or 
intervenors requested a hearing. As a result, the hearing was canceled. Notice of 
Cancelation of Hearing, June 7, 2024. On July 11, 2024, the Authority issued a proposed 
final decision and offered the parties and intervenors the chance to provide written 
exceptions. The Authority received no written exceptions. 
C. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 
The Authority recognized the following as parties to this proceeding: Alphonso L 
Coles, Brass City Community Television, Inc., 140 Fulkerson Drive, #3E, Waterbury, CT 
06708; Stephen W. Mindera, Jr., Skye Cable XIII, Inc., 117 Sharon Road, Waterbury, CT 
06705; Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement, Ten Franklin Square, New 
Britain, CT 06051; Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC), Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, 
CT 06051; and the Commissioner of the Department of Energy and Environmental 
Protection (DEEP), 79 Elm Street, Hartford, CT 06106. 
II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
General Statutes § 16-331a (l) provides that when “an organization assigned 
responsibility for community access operations which organization ceases to provide 
such operations” it “shall transfer its assets to the successor organization assigned such 

Docket No. 24-01-41 
Page 2 

responsibility or, if no successor organization is assigned such responsibility, to another 
nonprofit organization within the franchise area selected by the authority.” 
General Statutes § 16-331a(c) addresses the type of information the Authority 
must assess when a nonprofit seeks to take over community access operations from a 
multichannel video programming distributor (MVPD). The criteria for selection provides 
guidance to the Authority in this proceeding. The Authority reviews the following criteria 
in this docket: 
(1) The recommendations of the advisory council and of the municipalities 
in the franchise area; 
(2) a review of the organization's or the company's performance in providing 
community access programming; 
(3) the operating plan submitted by the organization and the company for 
providing community access programming; 
(4) the experience in community access programming of the organization; 
(5) the organization's and the company's proposed budget, including 
expenses for salaries, consultants, attorneys, and other professionals; 
(6) the quality and quantity of the programming to be created, promoted or 
facilitated by the organization or the company; 
(7) a review of the organization's procedures to ensure compliance with 
federal and state law, including the regulations of Connecticut state 
agencies; and 
(8) any other criteria determined to be relevant by the authority. 

General Statutes § 16-331a(c). “If the authority selects an organization to provide 
community access operations, the [MVPD] shall provide financial and technical support 
to the organization in an amount to be determined by the authority.” Id. 
III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
BRASS CITY APPLICATION 
Brass City is a community-based nonprofit entity, headquartered in Waterbury, 
which was established and registered with the Secretary of the State in February 2024 
and is spearheaded by Alphonso Coles, Brass City’s Executive Director. Petition, p. 1. 
Colleen Fitzpatrick serves as Brass City’s Program Director. Id. Brass City’s Petition sets 
forth the qualifications of Mr. Coles and Ms. Fitzpatrick, Brass City’s plan for operation, 
and its proposed community operations. The Authority addresses the eight guiding 
statutory criteria below. 
1. The recommendations of the advisory council and of the municipalities 
in the franchise area. 
Brass City’s Petition included a letter from the Greater Waterbury Cable Council 
(GWCC). Petition, Att. 4.1. GWCC endorsed Mr. Coles’ proposal to take over community 
access operations stating that “Al Coles is not only well-acquainted with the current 
operations at SKYE but also brings with him a network of quality professionals who have 
previously enriched SKYE with their administrative and instructional expertise.” Id. 

Docket No. 24-01-41 
Page 3 

GCWW acknowledged Mr. Coles’ “longstanding commitment to community service, as 
evidenced by his successful tenure at SKYE” along with his “comprehensive 
understanding of broadcast operations, combined with a practical approach to education 
and community engagement.” Id. GCWW opines that this makes Mr. Coles “an 
outstanding choice to helm these operations” and that Mr. Coles “possesses the 
leadership qualities necessary to fully realize the studio's potential as a hub for community 
enrichment through education and hands-on learning.” Id. The treasurer of the GWCC, 
Terrence S. McAuliffe, also provided an individual recommendation, which is addressed 
in Section III.A.8, below. 
2. A review of the organization's or the company's performance in 
providing community access programming. 
As this is a new nonprofit, the Authority does not have the ability to review the 
organization’s performance in providing community access programing. However, as 
discussed in Section III.A.4 below, Mr. Coles and Ms. Fitzgerald both have significant 
experience in community access operations and production from their tenure at Skye. 
The Authority is confident that the individual experiences can be properly imputed onto 
Brass City. 
3. The operating plan submitted by the organization and the company for 
providing community access programming. 
Brass City will be run by Mr. Coles, serving as Executive Director. Petition, p. 1. 
Mr. Coles has close to 35 years of experience in community access television, with 26 of 
those being with Skye. Id. Joining Mr. Coles is Ms. Fitzpatrick as Program Director. 
Petition, p. 1. Ms. Fitzpatrick has 18 years’ experience working in public access, including 
8 years at Skye. Id. Brass City plans to continue operations out of the current Skye 
location with uninterrupted access and with minimal to no down time or blackout period. 
Id., p. 2. Brass City also anticipates extending the hours the studio is open (currently half 
days on the weekends), to provide additional community outreach, especially to more 
underserved groups and communities, and to develop a more collaborative relationship 
with the local school administrations with the goal of having students creating content 
once again to air over the Educational Access channel. Id., p. 4. 
4. The experience in community access programming of the organization. 
As this is a new nonprofit, the Authority does not have the ability to review the 
organization’s experience in community access. However, Mr. Coles and Ms. Fitzgerald 
both have significant experience in community access operations and production from 
their tenure at Skye. The Authority is confident that this experience can be properly 
imputed onto Brass City. 
5. The organization's and the company's proposed budget, including 
expenses for salaries, consultants, attorneys, and other professionals. 
Brass City provided an estimated budget of $255,000, $245,000, and $235,000 for 
the years 2024 through 2026 in support of its petition. Petition, Att. 2, p. 1. The projection 
is based on Skye’s 2021 annual report (Skye’s most recently filed report). Id. Salaries 
are anticipated to be Brass City’s biggest expense at $140,000 for 2024 increasing to 

Docket No. 24-01-41 
Page 4 

$150,000 for 2025. Following salaries, rent, legal/professional fees, insurance, and 
telephones/utilities make up the largest expenses with totals ranging from $10,000 for 
insurance to $35,400 for rent in 2024, as an example. Id. The proposed budget is in line 
with Skye’s budget from previous years and shows moderate increases, which are not 
out of line with inflation. The budget submitted is reasonable under the circumstances 
and based on the best information available. 
6. The quality and quantity of the programming to be created, promoted or 
facilitated by the organization or the company. 
While the Petition does not go into depth on the quantity of programing to be 
created by Brass City, it does discuss facilitating increased educational content and 
continuing to strengthen ties with the local government for government content. Petition, 
p. 3. Brass City intends to revitalize educational content by working collaboratively with 
the Waterbury Arts Magnet School. Petition, p. 3. Brass City also intends to continue the 
Skye operations without interruption, indicating that the programing currently being 
produced will continue. Id., p. 2. Brass City also intends to “provide additional community 
outreach, especially to more underserved groups and communities, to foster a more 
inclusive environment, and promote a more diverse program lineup that reflects the 
diversity of the communities we serve.” Id., p. 3. 
7. A review of the organization's procedures to ensure compliance with 
federal and state law, including the regulations of Connecticut state 
agencies. 
Brass City is familiar with and is committed to complying with all federal and state 
laws. Petition, p. 4. Brass City also intends to continue the relationship Skye has with 
Kim Fisher, a nonprofit strategist/consultant, and to retain legal counsel as part of Brass 
City’s yearly budget. Id. Brass City’s Policies and Procedures reference and discuss 
relevant PURA regulations and demonstrate that Brass City is prepared to comply with 
applicable regulations. Id., Att. 3. 
8. Any other criteria determined to be relevant by the authority. 
The Authority concludes that no additional criteria must be examined at this time. 
However, the Authority notes that additional comments were received from the public. 
The Authority received correspondence from Attorney F. David Corbett who 
wholeheartedly offered his support for Mr. Coles. Corbett Corresp., May 1, 2024. 
Attorney Corbett taught Mr. Coles in the 1970s and also worked with him when Attorney 
Corbett had a community access show on Skye Cable from 1996 to 2015. Id. Attorney 
Corbett states that Mr. Coles is “a great mentor, teacher and leader” and that he cannot 
identify a person “more qualified to lead a public access station than Alphonso Coles.” Id. 
As mentioned above, the treasurer of the GWCC, Terrence S. McAuliffe, who is 
also the owner of Tribury Media, LLC, provided an individual letter of recommendation in 
addition to the GWCC letter. Petition, Att. 4.2. Mr. McAuliffe spoke of Mr. Coles’ “technical 
proficiency, combined with his profound commitment to fostering a community-centric 
broadcasting environment” as well as his “eagerness to mentor and educate community 
members and staff alike in the intricacies of media production” and his commitment to 
empowerment through education. Id. 

Docket No. 24-01-41 
Page 5 

IV. 
CONCLUSION AND ORDERS 
A. 
CONCLUSION 
A review of the materials presented by Brass City and in support of Brass City 
demonstrates that Brass City is well equipped to assume community access provider 
duties as Skye winds down its operation. As a result, the Authority directs Brass City to 
assume the Community Access Provider designation as well as the responsibilities for 
and the control of operations at the access facility, which are currently designated to and 
controlled by Skye. The Authority further directs Skye to work with Brass City to effectuate 
a smooth transfer of operations and assets. 
B. 
ORDERS 
For orders requiring a filing, Brass City shall file an electronic version through the 
Authority’s website at www.ct.gov/pura. Submissions filed in compliance with the 
Authority’s orders must be identified by: Docket Number, Title, and Order Number. 
Compliance with orders shall commence and continue as indicated in each specific order 
or until Brass City requests and the Authority approves that Brass City’s compliance is no 
longer required after a certain date. Unless otherwise provided or determined by the 
Authority, filings submitted in compliance with an order shall constitute satisfaction of the 
order. Filings requiring Authority approval must be filed as a motion. 
1. 
Skye and Brass City are directed to work together to effectuate smooth transfer of 
both the community access operations and the assets identified by Skye. 
2. 
Upon the completion of the transfer, Brass City shall file compliance in this docket 
indicating that it has assumed Skye’s community access provider duties. 
3. 
Upon completion of the transfer, Brass City shall provide written confirmation to its 
area MVPDs to alert them to the transfer of duties and to ensure the smooth 
transfer of the MVPDs support obligations. 
4. 
Following the completion of the transfer, Brass City is directed to file an 
appearance in any active Authority docket in which Skye currently is a party, 
participant, or intervenor to alert all docket participant of the transfer. The 
appearance shall indicate that any communications or filings previously directed 
to Skye should thereafter be directed to Brass City. This includes but is not limited 
to the Annual Allocation of Public Educational and Governmental Programming 
and Education Technology Investment Account (Docket No. 23-10-02) the Annual 
Community Access Support docket (Docket No. 24-01-06). 

DOCKET NO. 24-01-41 
REQUEST 
TO 
TRANSFER 
COMMUNITY 
ACCESS PROVIDER DESIGNATION 

This Decision is adopted by the following Commissioners: 

Marissa P. Gillett 

John W. Betkoski, III 

Michael A. Caron

Utilities Regulatory Authority, State of Connecticut, and was forwarded by Certified Mail 
to all parties of record in this proceeding on the date indicated.

STATE OF CONNECTICUT

THE PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY

May 29, 2024 

By the following Commissioners:

DECISION 

TABLE OF CONTENTS 
I. 
INTRODUCTION .......................................................................................................... 1 
A. SUMMARY ................................................................................................................ 1 
B. BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING .......................................................................... 1 
C. CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING ................................................................................ 1

A. CONCLUSION ............................................................................................................ 3

APPENDIX A – 2024 SUBSCRIBER FEE……………………………………………………i 
APPENDIX B – CONNECTICUT FRANCHISE/SERVICE AREAS……………………….ii 
APPENDIX C – SERVICE LIST………………………………………………………………iv 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
In this Decision, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) 
establishes the inflation-adjusted amount of community access support required pursuant 
to General Statutes § 16-331a(k). The consumer price index (CPI)1 for the 2023 inflation 
rate is 2.59%. The Authority uses this number to determine the 2024 inflation-adjusted 
amounts of community access support required from all multichannel video programming 
distributors. 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
The General Assembly requires the provision of “facilities, equipment, and 
technical and managerial support to enable the production of meaningful community 
access programming within [each] franchise area.” General Statutes § 16-331a(b). 
Through an annual proceeding, the Authority determines “the amount that the company 
or organization responsible for community access operations shall receive for such 
operations from subscribers and from multichannel video programming distributors.” 
General Statutes § 16-331a(k). 
Holders of a Certificate of Cable Franchise Authority (CCFA) or Certificate of Video 
Franchise Authority (CVFA) are required to provide funds in the amount established by 
the Authority. 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On its own motion, the Authority established this docket on January 26, 2024. The 
Authority delegated this matter to its Office of Education, Outreach, and Enforcement 
(EOE). Notice of Proceeding, p. 1. 
EOE filed a motion to approve a Proposed Final Decision on April 11, 2024. 
Participants had seven days from the filing of EOE’s motion to review the proposed 
decision and to file objections to the motion. 
On April 25, 2024, the Authority issued a Proposed Final Decision. All participants 
were given the opportunity to file written exceptions to the Proposed Final Decision. 
Exceptions were filed by numerous community access providers and letters in lieu were 
filed by multichannel video programming distributors (MVPD). Pursuant to Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-10(b), MVPDs have 30 days after notification of the adjusted 
amount per subscriber if they believe the calculation is incorrect. 
D. 
PARTICIPANTS AND INTERVENORS 
The Authority designated the Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC), Ten Franklin 
Square, New Britain, Connecticut 06051; the Commissioner of the Department of Energy 

1 Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-1(2) defines the consumer price index as the United States Department 
of Labor Consumer Price Index, Urban Northeast Region, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. 

Docket No. 24-01-06 

Page 2 

and Environmental Protection (DEEP Commissioner) 79 Elm Street, Hartford, 
Connecticut 06106; EOE, Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, Connecticut 06051, and all 
Connecticut MVPDs and community access providers as participants to this proceeding. 
All Connecticut cable advisory councils were designated intervenors. A listing of all 
participants and intervenors is appended hereto as Appendix C.2 
II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
By June 1 of each year, PURA establishes the amount of funding for community 
access operations for each franchise area. General Statutes § 16-331a(k); Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-10. The amount of funding is determined by adjusting the 
prior year amount by the CPI for the preceding calendar year. Id.3 

After considering certain criteria, the Authority may increase or decrease this 
amount within a range of 40% of the inflation adjusted subscriber fee. Id. When 
evaluating whether to increase or decrease the per-subscriber amount, the Authority shall 
consider the factors articulated in Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-8. 
III. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
CPI CALCULATION 

The Authority determines herein: (1) the 2023 rate of inflation as measured by the 
CPI for the Northeast Urban Region; (2) the 2024 franchise-specific community access 
support per subscriber amounts; and (3) whether the amounts are within +/-40% of the 
allowed statutory amount, as adjusted for inflation. 
The index values for determining the rate of inflation for 2023 as measured by the 
CPI4 for the Northeast Urban Region are as follows: 
Year 
Dec. 
2022 
308.150 
2023 
316.143 

Based on this data, the 2023 rate of inflation for updating community access 
support amounts pursuant to General Statutes § 16-331a(k) is 2.59%. Since the CPI for 
the Northeast Urban Region increased 2.59% during 2023, the community access 
support amounts are increased by 2.59% as shown in Appendix A. To determine the +/-
40% range within which the Authority may change the per subscriber amount, the 
Authority adjusts the original statutory $5 per subscriber, as adjusted yearly, by the 
inflation adjustment. In the 2023 Decision, the Authority found that the statutory amount 
as adjusted for inflation was $10.82. Increasing this amount by 2.59% for 2023 CPI 

2 The Authority requests that all participants inform the Authority of any changes/additions to the names, 
addresses and /or titles in the Appendix C service list by filing correspondence in this docket. 
3 The General Assembly set the initial amount at five dollars per subscriber per year. 
4 See https://www.bls.gov/regions/mid-atlantic/data/consumerpriceindexhistorical_northeast_table.htm. 

Docket No. 24-01-06 

Page 3 

inflation equates to a value of $11.10. Forty percent of $11.10 is $4.44. Consequently, 
the community access support per subscriber must be between $6.66 ($11.10 – $4.44) 
and $15.54 ($11.10 + $4.44). Appendix A demonstrates that the subscriber amounts are 
properly within this range. 
For the MVPDs “the amount shall be paid on a quarterly basis and shall be 
determined by multiplying the amount per subscriber by the average number of 
subscribers as determined in section 16-331a-9.” Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-7. 
Each MVPD will be ordered to fund community access in 2024 at the inflation-adjusted 
per-subscriber amount shown in Appendix A. 
B. 
REQUESTS FOR INCREASE 
In this docket, the Authority does not order an increase beyond the CPI of last 
year’s total figure for each MVPD as set forth in Appendix A. Many community access 
providers requested that the Authority increase their subscriber fees to the $15.54 
maximum allowed within the 40% range. See, e.g. Branford Community Television 
Written Exceptions, May 8, 2024, p. 1. Many of the community access providers also 
provided numbers showing that the amount the community access providers received in 
funding through subscriber fees has been declining in recent years, other than 2022 
when the Authority ordered an increase. See, e.g., Totoket TV Written Exceptions, p. 2. 
Conversely, Charter Communications of Northeastern Connecticut and Charter 
Communications of Western Connecticut (Charter) states that the level of support 
provided in the Western Connecticut area has “exceeded that necessary to support 
meaningful community access” and requests an order for Charter to engage in informal 
discussions with EOE to consider the surcharge level going forward. Charter Written 
Exceptions, p. 1. 
The Authority declines to exercise its discretion to further adjust the subscriber fee 
in this year’s annual docket as the records lacks substantial evidence on which to base 
such a decision, and because PURA has received no further legislative direction to do 
so. The Authority also declines to issue an order as requested by Charter.5 
IV. 
CONCLUSION AND ORDERS 
A. 
CONCLUSION 
The increase in the CPI for the Northeast Urban Region during calendar year 2023 
is 2.59%. The franchise-specific inflation adjustments calculated in this Decision apply to 
all Connecticut MVPDs and community access providers. The 2024 Subscriber Fee 
required of each MVPD is set forth in Appendix A. 

5 Charter, like all participants, may engage in discussions with EOE (which is also a participant in these 
proceedings) without an order from the Authority. 

Docket No. 24-01-06 

Page 4 

B. 
ORDERS 
For the following Orders, participants shall file electronic versions through the 
Authority’s website at www.ct.gov/pura. Submissions filed in compliance with the 
Authority’s Orders must be identified by all three of the following: Docket Number, Title 
and Order Number. Compliance with orders shall commence and continue as indicated 
in each specific Order or until a participant requests and the Authority approves that the 
compliance is no longer required after a certain date. Unless otherwise provided or 
determined by the Authority, filings submitted in compliance with an order shall constitute 
satisfaction of the order. Filings requiring Authority approval must be filed as a motion. 
1. 
Effective July 1, 2024, and continuing for twelve (12) months, each MVPD shall 
fund community access using the 2024 Subscriber Fee shown in Appendix A for 
each franchise service area in which it provides video service. Frontier shall fund 
community access using the 2024 Subscriber Fee shown in Appendix A for each 
franchise service area in which it provides video service, and shall file, as a 
compliance filing, the Subscriber Fee and total amount paid for each franchise 
service area in which it provides service. 
2. 
All Advisory Councils shall file their 2024 Annual Report no later than January 31, 
2025, under the current Docket Number. 
3. 
All Community Access Providers shall file their 2024 Community Access Report 
no later than February 15, 2025, under the current Docket Number. 
4. 
The designated community access providers, advisory councils, parties, 
intervenors, and MVPDs shall inform the Authority of any changes/additions to the 
names, addresses and /or titles in the Appendix C service list.

DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) allocates $3,006,596 
in grants from the Public, Educational and Governmental Programming and Education 
Technology Investment Account (PEGPETIA). The Authority awards PEGPETIA funds 
accumulated through February 22, 2024, in this proceeding, with $1,503,301 for 39 grants 
to support public, educational, and governmental programming (PEG Grants) and 
$1,503,295 for 74 grants to support educational technology initiatives (ETI Grants). 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
In 2007, the General Assembly established the PEGPETIA program to promote 
and improve public, educational, and governmental programming and to support 
education technology initiatives. See Public Act No. 07-253, § 33, codified as General 
Statutes § 16-331cc. The program is funded by a quarterly tax on the gross earnings of 
video service providers. General Statutes § 16-331cc. 
The Authority conducts an annual proceeding to determine the allocation of the 
accumulated funding in the account and to administer grants to eligible entities. The 
Authority established the application requirements through a contested proceeding in 
2008 and revised the requirements in 2019. Decision, Mar. 26, 2008, Docket No. 07-10-

II. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA 
The Authority awards 50% of PEGPETIA grant funding to: (1) local community 
antenna television and video advisory councils; (2) the state-wide video advisory council; 
(3) public, educational, and governmental programmers; and (4) public, educational, and 
governmental studio operators, “to subsidize capital and equipment costs related to 
producing and procuring [public, educational and governmental] programming.” General 
Statutes § 16-331cc(b). The Authority awards the remaining 50% “to boards of education 
and other education entities for education technology initiatives.” Id. 
The PEG grant funding is intended to promote and improve public, educational, 
and governmental access programming in Connecticut. Guidelines Decision, p. 2. 
Although funds are available to a wide variety of entities involved either directly or 
indirectly in producing community access programs, the awarding of funds to those 
entities is not the goal of the program. Id. PEG grant funds should be used for capital 
and equipment costs that aid the production or procurement of public, educational, and 
governmental programs. Accordingly, after receiving a PEG grant, recipients must file a 
report with the Authority, stating: (a) the title, subject, and duration (in minutes) of all 
community access programs facilitated in whole or in part by the grant award; (b) how the 
programs were distributed through community access channels; and (c) the protocols for 
ensuring that any programs produced with equipment purchased with PEGPETIA funds 
are made available to the applicant’s local PEG studio. To ensure the funding is used 
appropriately, after completion of the project, PEG grant recipients must also file a report 
of the project enabled by the grant funds. 
The ETI grant funding is intended to support education technology initiatives of 
boards of education and other education entities. Both public and private schools are 
eligible to apply for PEGPETIA funds. Guidelines Decision, p. 14. To ensure the funding 
is used appropriately, after completion of the project, ETI grant recipients must file a report 
of the project enabled by the grant funds. 
B. 
APPLICATIONS AND ELIGIBILITY REVIEW 
In this docket, 117 applications were submitted, including 41 applications for PEG 
Grants and 76 applications for ETI Grants. The Authority awards a total of $1,503,301 in 
39 PEG Grants and a total of $1,503,295 in 74 ETI Grants. The PEG grants support the 
promotion and improvement of public, educational, and governmental programming, and 
the ETI grants support education technology initiatives. General Statutes § 16-331cc.

ages 3-5. In its application, the Children’s Center sought funding for 2 iPad pro tablets

C. 
ALLOCATION OF PEGPETIA FUNDS 
For the grant cycle in this docket, $3,006,662 is available in the PEGPETIA 
account. The Authority awards half of the funding in PEG Grants for capital and 
equipment costs related to producing and procuring public, educational and governmental 
programming, and the Authority awards half of the funding in ETI Grants for education 
technology initiatives. General Statutes § 16-331cc(b). PEG Grants are available to (1) 
local community antenna television and video advisory councils, (2) the state-wide video 
advisory council (3) public, educational, and governmental programmers, and (4) public, 
educational, and governmental studio operators. Id. ETI Grants are available to boards 
of education and other education entities. Id. 
The Authority received 117 applications for PEGPETIA grants, with 4 applicants 
deemed wholly ineligible. The 39 eligible PEG Grant applicants sought a total of 
$4,348,165.63 for public, educational, and governmental programming. The 74 eligible 
ETI Grant applicants sought $11,161,306.75 for education technology initiatives. Over 
20% of the budget items in those applications were for costs that are ineligible for 
PEGPETIA funding, such as expenses for permitting, travel, lodging, and salaries. See 
Guidelines Decision, pp. 3-4. PEGPETIA grant funds may not be used on non-equipment 
costs such as salaries, service agreements, or stipends. As noted in the application, non-
equipment costs, such as design and engineering, installation, training, warranties, or 
insurance, must be reasonable and should be limited to less than 10% of the overall grant. 
Software may be categorized as equipment.
